topics.title: Page 27
topics.context:
When the magneto check is performed, a drop in torquemeter pressure indication is a good supplement to the variation in rpm. In cases where the tachometer scale is graduated coarsely, the torquemeter variation may give more positive evidence of the power change when switching to the individual magneto condition. A loss in torquemeter pressure not to exceed 10 percent can be expected when operating on a single magneto. By comparing the rpm drop with a known standard, the following are determined:
1. Proper timing of each magneto.
2. General engine performance as evidenced by smooth operation.
3. Additional check of the proper connection of the ignition leads.
Any unusual roughness on either magneto is an indication of faulty ignition caused by plug fouling or by malfunctioning of the ignition system. The operator should be very sensitive to engine roughness during this check. Lack of dropoff in rpm may be an indication of faulty grounding of one side of the ignition system. Complete cutting out when switching to one magneto is definite evidence that its side of the ignition system is not functioning. Excessive difference in rpm drop off between the left and right switch positions can indicate a difference in time between the left and right magnetos.
Sufficient time should be given to the check on each single switch position to permit complete stabilization of engine speed and manifold pressure. There is a tendency to perform this check too rapidly with resultant wrong indications. Operation as long as 1 minute on a single ignition system is not excessive.
Another point that must be emphasized is the danger of sticking tachometer. The tachometer should be tapped lightly to make sure the indicator needle moves freely. In some cases using older mechanical tachometers, sticking has caused errors in indication to the extent of 100 rpm. Under such conditions, the ignition system could have had as much as a 200 rpm drop with only a 100 rpm drop indicated on the instrument. In most cases, tapping the instrument eliminates the sticking and results in accurate readings.
In recording the results of time ignition system check, record the amount of the total rpm drop that occurs rapidly and the amount that occurs slowly. This breakdown in rpm drop provides a means of pinpointing certain troubles in the ignition system. This can reduce unnecessary work by confining maintenance to the specific part of the ignition system that is responsible for the trouble.
Fast rpm drop is usually the result of either faulty spark plugs or faulty ignition harness. This is true because faulty plugs or leads, take effect at once. The cylinder goes dead or starts firing intermittently the instant the switch is moved from “both” to the “right” or “left” position.
Slow rpm drop usually is caused by incorrect ignition timing or faulty valve adjustment. With late ignition timing, the charge is fired too late (in relation to piston travel) for the combustion pressures to build up to the maximum at the proper time. The result is a power loss greater than normal for single ignition because of the lower peak pressures obtained in the cylinder. However, this power loss does not occur as rapidly as that which accompanies a dead spark plug. This explains the slow rpm drop as compared to the instantaneous drop with a dead plug or defective lead. Incorrect valve clearances, through their effect on valve overlap, can cause the mixture to be too rich or too lean. The too rich or too lean mixture may affect one plug more than another, because of the plug location and show up as a slow rpm drop on the ignition check. Switch from “both” to “right” and return to “both.” Switch from “both” to “left” and return to “both.” Observe the rpm drop while operating on the right and left positions. The maximum drop should not exceed that specified by the engine manufacturer.
**Fuel Pressure & Oil Pressure Check**
Fuel pressure and oil pressure must be within the established tolerance (green arc) for the engine.
**Propeller Pitch Check**
The propeller is checked to ensure proper operation of the pitch control and the pitch-change mechanism. The operation of a controllable pitch propeller is checked by the indications of the tachometer and manifold pressure gauge when the propeller governor control is moved from one position to another. Because each type of propeller requires a different procedure, the applicable manufacturer’s instructions should be followed.
**Power Check**
Specific rpm and manifold pressure relationship should be checked during each ground check. This can be done at the time the engine is run-up to make the magneto check. The purpose of this check is to measure the performance of the engine against an established standard. Calibration tests have determined that the engine is capable of delivering a given power at a given rpm and manifold pressure. The original calibration, or measurement of power, is made by means of a dynamometer in a test cell. During the ground check, power is measured with the propeller. With constant conditions of air density, the propeller, at any fixed-pitch position, always requires the same rpm to absorb the same horsepower from the engine. This characteristic is used in determining the condition of the engine.

faqs.question: What indicates a proper magneto check when switching to a single magneto?
faqs.answer: A drop in torquemeter pressure not exceeding 10 % and a corresponding rpm drop that matches the known standard indicate a proper magneto check.

faqs.question: How can I tell if the ignition timing of a magneto is incorrect?
faqs.answer: A slow rpm drop when the magneto is switched to single‑ignition suggests incorrect ignition timing, as the power loss occurs gradually rather than instantly.

faqs.question: What does a fast rpm drop during the magneto check usually mean?
faqs.answer: A fast rpm drop is usually caused by a faulty spark plug or a defective ignition lead, which affect engine power instantly when the switch is moved.

faqs.question: Why is it important to tap the tachometer lightly during the check?
faqs.answer: Tapping the tachometer ensures the needle moves freely; a sticking tachometer can under‑report rpm drops by up to 100 rpm, leading to inaccurate assessment of the ignition system.

faqs.question: What should I observe if there is no rpm drop when switching to a single magneto?
faqs.answer: A lack of rpm drop may indicate faulty grounding of one side of the ignition system.

faqs.question: How long should I allow the engine to stabilize on each single‑magneto position?
faqs.answer: Allow up to one minute on each single‑ignition position to let engine speed and manifold pressure fully stabilize before recording measurements.

faqs.question: What does an excessive difference in rpm drop between left and right magneto positions suggest?
faqs.answer: It can indicate a timing difference between the left and right magnetos.

faqs.question: What are the key items to check during the fuel and oil pressure inspection?
faqs.answer: Both fuel pressure and oil pressure must be within the manufacturer‑specified tolerance (green arc) for the engine.

faqs.question: How is the propeller pitch control verified during a ground check?
faqs.answer: By observing the tachometer and manifold pressure indications while moving the propeller governor control; the procedure follows the specific propeller manufacturer’s instructions.

faqs.question: What is the purpose of the power check performed during the magneto run‑up?
faqs.answer: The power check compares the engine’s rpm‑manifold pressure relationship to the established standard, using the propeller’s known rpm requirement for a given horsepower to assess engine performance.

summary.title: Magneto Check and Engine Performance Diagnostic Procedure
summary.long_summary:
The magneto check evaluates engine health by observing torquemeter pressure and RPM changes when switching to a single magneto. A torquemeter pressure drop of up to 10 % is normal; the accompanying RPM reduction, compared with a known standard, reveals proper magneto timing, overall engine smoothness, and correct ignition lead connections. Roughness on either magneto indicates plug fouling or ignition system faults, while a missing RPM drop suggests poor grounding. Complete loss of power on one magneto confirms that side’s failure, and unequal RPM drops between left and right positions point to timing differences.

The test must allow the engine speed and manifold pressure to stabilize—typically up to one minute per magneto—to avoid erroneous readings. Tachometer stickiness can mask true RPM changes; a light tap frees the needle and restores accuracy. When recording results, separate the rapid RPM drop (usually caused by faulty spark plugs or ignition harnesses) from the slower drop (often due to incorrect ignition timing or improper valve adjustment). Fast drops occur instantly as the cylinder misfires; slow drops stem from late ignition timing or valve‑clearance issues that affect combustion pressure and mixture richness.

After the magneto check, verify fuel and oil pressures are within the manufacturer‑specified green arc. Inspect propeller pitch operation by monitoring tachometer and manifold‑pressure indications while moving the governor control, following the specific propeller’s manual. Finally, conduct a power check by correlating RPM with manifold pressure during ground run‑up. Since a fixed‑pitch propeller absorbs a constant horsepower at a given RPM under constant air‑density conditions, deviations from calibrated RPM‑pressure values indicate a change in engine performance.

Afterfiring

Afterfiring, sometimes called afterburning, often results when the air-fuel mixture is too rich. Overly rich mixtures are also slow burning; therefore, charges of unburned fuel are present in the exhausted gases. Air from outside the exhaust stacks mixes with this unburned fuel that ignites. This causes an explosion in the exhaust system. Afterfiring is perhaps more common where long exhaust ducting retains greater amounts of unburned charges. As in the case of backfiring, the correction for afterfiring is the proper adjustment of the air-fuel mixture.

Afterfiring can also be caused by cylinders that are not firing because of faulty spark plugs, defective fuel-injection nozzles, or incorrect valve clearance. The unburned mixture from these dead cylinders passes into the exhaust system, where it ignites and burns. Unfortunately, the resultant torching or afterburning can easily be mistaken for evidence of a rich carburetor. Cylinders that are firing intermittently can cause a similar effect. Again, the malfunction can be remedied only by discovering the real cause and correcting the defect. Dead or intermittent cylinders can be located by the cold cylinder check.

Factors Affecting Engine Operation

Compression

To prevent loss of power, all openings to the cylinder must close and seal completely on the compression and power strokes. In this respect, there are three items in the proper operation of the cylinder that must be operating correctly for maximum efficiency. First, the piston rings must be in good condition to provide maximum sealing during the stroke of the piston. There must be no leakage between the piston and the walls of the combustion chamber. Second, the intake and exhaust valves must close tightly so that there is no loss of compression at these points. Third, and very important, the timing of the valves (opening and closing) must be such that highest efficiency is obtained when the engine is operating at its normal rated rpm. A failure at any of these points results in greatly reduced engine efficiency.

Fuel Metering

The induction system is the distribution and fuel-metering part of the engine. Obviously, any defect in the induction system seriously affects engine operation. For best operation, each cylinder of the engine must be provided with the proper air-fuel mixture, usually metered by the carburetor. On some fuel-injection engines, fuel is metered by the fuel injector flow divider and fuel-injection nozzles.

The relation between air-fuel ratio and power is illustrated in Figure 10-44. As the fuel mixture is varied from lean to rich, the power output of the engine increases until it reaches a maximum. Beyond this point, the power output falls off as the mixture is further enriched. This is because the fuel mixture is now too rich to provide perfect combustion. Note that maximum engine power can be obtained by setting the carburetor for one point on the curve.

In establishing the carburetor settings for an aircraft engine, the design engineers run a series of curves similar to the one shown. A curve is run for each of several engine speeds. If, for example, the idle speed is 600 rpm, the first curve might be run at this speed. Another curve might be run at 700 rpm, another at 800 rpm, and so on, in 100-rpm increments, up to takeoff rpm. The points of maximum power on the curves are then joined to obtain the best power curve of the engine for all speeds. This best power curve establishes the rich setting of the carburetor.

In establishing the detailed engine requirements regarding carburetor setting, the fact that the cylinder head temperature varies with air-fuel ratio must be considered. This variation is illustrated in the curve shown in Figure 10-45. Note that the cylinder head temperature is lower with the auto-lean setting than it is with the auto-rich mixture. This is exactly opposite common belief, but it is true. Furthermore, knowledge of this fact can be used to advantage by flight crews. If, during cruise, it becomes difficult to keep the cylinder head temperature within limits, the air-fuel mixture may be leaned out to get cooler operation. The desired cooling can then be obtained without going to auto-rich with its costly waste of fuel. The curve shows only the variation in cylinder head temperature. For a given rpm, the power output of the engine is less with the best-economy setting (auto-lean) than with the best-power mixture.

faqs.question: What is afterfiring and why does it occur?
faqs.answer: Afterfiring, also called afterburning, occurs when unburned fuel in the exhaust mixes with outside air and ignites, causing an explosion in the exhaust system. It is often the result of an overly rich air‑fuel mixture or cylinders that are not firing properly.

faqs.question: How can a rich carburetor be distinguished from afterfiring caused by dead cylinders?
faqs.answer: Both can produce a torching effect in the exhaust, but afterfiring caused by dead or intermittent cylinders is due to unburned mixture from those cylinders. The real cause must be identified—such as checking for faulty spark plugs, defective fuel‑injection nozzles, or incorrect valve clearance—rather than assuming a rich carburetor.

faqs.question: What engine components must be in good condition to maintain proper compression?
faqs.answer: The piston rings must seal the cylinder walls, the intake and exhaust valves must close tightly, and the valve timing must be correct for the engine’s rated rpm. Failure of any of these results in reduced engine efficiency.

faqs.question: Why is valve timing important for engine efficiency?
faqs.answer: Valve timing determines when the valves open and close. Proper timing ensures the highest efficiency at the engine’s normal rated rpm; incorrect timing leads to loss of compression and reduced power.

faqs.question: How does the air‑fuel ratio affect engine power according to the power‑versus‑mixture curve?
faqs.answer: Power increases as the mixture moves from lean toward rich, reaches a maximum at the optimal (auto‑rich) ratio, and then falls off if the mixture becomes too rich for perfect combustion.

faqs.question: What is the purpose of running multiple power‑versus‑mixture curves at different engine speeds?
faqs.answer: Engine designers run curves at various rpm (e.g., 600, 700, 800 rpm, etc.) to locate the point of maximum power for each speed. Connecting these points creates the best‑power curve, which defines the carburetor’s rich setting for the whole operating range.

faqs.question: How does the air‑fuel mixture influence cylinder head temperature?
faqs.answer: A leaner (auto‑lean) mixture results in a lower cylinder head temperature than an auto‑rich mixture. This relationship holds through the normal cruise range; at higher power settings, cylinder temperatures rise.

faqs.question: Can leaning the mixture during cruise help control cylinder head temperature?
faqs.answer: Yes. If cylinder head temperature is too high during cruise, leaning the mixture cools the engine without switching to the auto‑rich setting, which would waste fuel.

faqs.question: What is the “cold cylinder check” used for?
faqs.answer: The cold cylinder check is a method to locate dead or intermittently firing cylinders, which can cause afterfiring by allowing unburned fuel to enter the exhaust.

summary.title: Afterfiring, Compression, and Fuel Metering in Aircraft Engines
summary.long_summary:
Afterfiring (or afterburning) occurs when unburned fuel in the exhaust ignites, often because the air‑fuel mixture is too rich or because one or more cylinders fail to fire due to faulty spark plugs, fuel‑injection nozzles, or incorrect valve clearance. The resulting explosion in the exhaust can be mistaken for a rich‑carburetor condition; the proper remedy is to correct the underlying mixture or cylinder defect, which can be diagnosed with a cold‑cylinder check.

Engine efficiency also depends on proper compression. The piston rings must seal the cylinder walls, intake and exhaust valves must close tightly, and valve timing must match the engine’s rated rpm. Any failure in these areas reduces power.

Fuel metering is handled by the induction system—carburetor in many engines or fuel‑injector flow dividers and nozzles in fuel‑injection engines. Power varies with the air‑fuel ratio: it rises from lean to an optimal rich point, then falls as the mixture becomes excessively rich. Engineers plot power curves at various rpms to locate the maximum‑power point and set the carburetor accordingly. 

Cylinder‑head temperature also changes with mixture. Counter‑intuitively, a leaner (auto‑lean) setting produces lower head temperatures than an auto‑rich setting, useful for cooling during cruise without sacrificing fuel efficiency. However, at high power settings, temperatures rise again. Understanding these relationships allows pilots to adjust mixtures for optimal power, economy, and temperature control while avoiding afterfiring and other combustion problems.

when the engine is running. However, the turbine wheels are relatively massive, compared with the case, and are not cooled so readily. The turbine case is exposed to cooling air from both inside and outside the engine. Consequently, the case and the wheels lose their residual heat at different rates after the engine has been shut down. The case, cooling faster, tends to shrink upon the wheels, that are still rotating. Under extreme conditions, the turbine blades may squeal or seize; thus, a cooling period is required if the engine has been operating at prolonged high speed. Should the turbine wheels seize, no harm normally results, provided no attempt is made to turn the engine over until it has cooled sufficiently to free the wheels. In spite of this, every effort should be made to avoid seizure.

To ensure that fuel remains in the lines and that the engine-driven fuel pumps are not starved for fuel that lubricates the pumps, the aircraft fuel boost pump must be turned off after, not before, the throttle or the fuel shutoff lever is placed in the OFF position.

Generally, an engine should not be shut down by the fuel shutoff lever until after the aircraft throttle has been retarded to idle. Because the fuel shutoff valve is located on the fuel control discharge, a shutdown from high thrust settings results in high fuel pressures within the control that can harm the fuel system parts.

When an accurate reading of the oil level in the oil tank is needed following an engine shutdown, the engine should be operated and shut down with the oil check taking place within not more than 30 minutes after shutdown. Check the engine manuals for the specific procedure.

### Troubleshooting Turbine Engines

Included in this section are typical guidelines for locating engine malfunctions on most turbine engines. Since it would be impractical to list all the malfunctions that could occur, only the most common malfunctions are covered. A thorough knowledge of the engine systems, applied with logical reasoning, solves most problems that may occur.

Figure 10-75 enumerates some malfunctions that may be encountered. Possible causes and suggested actions are given in the adjacent columns. The malfunctions presented herein are solely for the purpose of illustration and should not be construed to have general application. For exact information about a specific engine model, consult the applicable manufacturer's instructions.

### Turboprop Operation

Turboprop engine operation is quite similar to that of a turbojet engine, except for the added feature of a propeller. The starting procedure and the various operational features are very much alike. The turboprop chiefly requires attention to engine operating limits, the throttle or power lever setting, and the torquemeter pressure gauge. Although torquemeters indicate only the power being supplied to the propeller and not the equivalent shaft horsepower, torquemeter pressure is approximately proportional to the total power output and, thus, is used as a measure of engine performance. The torquemeter pressure gauge reading during the takeoff engine check is an important value. It is usually necessary to compute the takeoff power in the same manner as is done for a turbojet engine. This computation is to determine the maximum allowable exhaust gas temperature and the torquemeter pressure that a normally functioning engine should produce for the outside, or ambient, air temperature and barometric pressure prevailing at the time.

### Troubleshooting Procedures for Turboprop Engines

All test run-ups, inspections, and troubleshooting should be performed in accordance with the applicable engine manufacturer's instructions. In Figure 10-76, the troubleshooting procedure for the turboprop reduction gear, torquemeter, and power section are combined because of their inter-relationships. The table includes the principal troubles, together with their probable causes and remedies.

### Turbine Engine Calibration & Testing

Some of the most important factors affecting turbine engine life are EGT, engine cycles (a cycle is generally a takeoff and landing) and engine speed. Excess EGT of a few degrees reduces turbine component life. Low EGT materially reduces turbine engine efficiency and thrust. So, to make the engine highly efficient, the exhaust temperatures need to be as high as possible, while maintaining an EGT operating temperature that does not damage the turbine section of the engine. If the engine is operated at excess exhaust temperatures, engine deterioration occurs. Since the EGT temperature is set by the EGT temperature gauge, it is imperative that it is accurate. Excessive engine speed can cause premature engine wear and, if extreme, can cause engine failure.

One older type of calibration test unit used to analyze the turbine engine is the jetcal analyzer. [Figure 10-77] A jetcal analyzer is a portable instrument made of aluminum, stainless steel, and plastic. The major components of the analyzer are the thermocouple, rpm, EGT indicator, resistance, and insulation check circuits, as well as the potentiometer, temperature regulators, meters, switches, and all the necessary cables, probes, and adapters for performing all tests.

faqs.question: Why must the turbine wheels be allowed to cool before attempting to turn the engine after shutdown?
faqs.answer: The turbine case cools faster than the massive turbine wheels, causing the case to shrink around the still‑hot wheels. If the wheels are still rotating or hot, they may squeal or seize. faqs.question: What can happen if turbine wheels seize, and is any damage expected?

faqs.question: When should the aircraft fuel boost pump be turned off relative to the throttle or fuel shutoff lever?
faqs.answer: The fuel boost pump must be turned off **after** the throttle or fuel shutoff lever is placed in the OFF position, to ensure fuel remains in the lines and the engine‑driven fuel pumps are not starved of lubricating fuel.

faqs.question: Why should the engine not be shut down by the fuel shutoff lever until after the throttle has been retarded to idle?
faqs.answer: Because the fuel shutoff valve is located on the fuel control discharge, shutting down from a high‑thrust setting creates high fuel pressures that can damage fuel‑system components.

faqs.question: When is the appropriate time to check the oil level in the oil tank after an engine shutdown?
faqs.answer: The oil level should be checked within **30 minutes** after shutdown, after the engine has been operated and shut down according to the specific procedure in the engine manual.

faqs.question: What is the purpose of the troubleshooting guidelines for turbine engines provided in the text?
faqs.answer: The guidelines give typical methods for locating common malfunctions on most turbine engines, using logical reasoning and knowledge of engine systems to solve most problems, though exact procedures should follow the specific manufacturer’s instructions.

faqs.question: How is torquemeter pressure used in turboprop engine operation?
faqs.answer: Torquemeter pressure indicates the power being supplied to the propeller and is approximately proportional to total power output. It is used as a measure of engine performance, especially during the take‑off engine check, to compute allowable exhaust gas temperature and torquemeter pressure for the prevailing ambient conditions.

faqs.question: Why is accurate EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature) measurement important for turbine engine life and performance?
faqs.answer: Excess EGT reduces turbine component life, while low EGT reduces efficiency and thrust. Maintaining EGT within the specified operating temperature maximizes engine efficiency and prevents premature wear or failure.

faqs.question: What is a JetCal analyzer and what are its main components?
faqs.answer: A JetCal analyzer is a portable turbine‑engine calibration test unit made of aluminum, stainless steel, and plastic. Its major components include a thermocouple, rpm and EGT indicators, resistance and insulation check circuits, a potentiometer, temperature regulators, meters, switches, and the necessary cables, probes, and adapters for performing all tests.

summary.title: Turbine Engine Shutdown, Operation, and Troubleshooting Guidelines
summary.long_summary:
The passage outlines essential procedures and considerations for turbine and turboprop engines. During shutdown, turbine wheels retain heat longer than the surrounding case, causing differential contraction that can lead to blade squeal or seizure; a cooling period is therefore required after prolonged high‑speed operation, and the engine should not be turned over until the wheels have cooled. Fuel system safety dictates that the aircraft fuel boost pump be turned off only after the throttle or fuel shutoff lever is placed in the OFF position, and the throttle should be retarded to idle before using the fuel shutoff lever to avoid high pressure damage. For accurate post‑shutdown oil level checks, the measurement must be taken within 30 minutes of engine stop, following the specific aircraft manual. 

Troubleshooting guidelines emphasize a systematic, logical approach based on a solid understanding of engine systems, with typical malfunctions illustrated in figures (e.g., Fig. 10‑75) and associated causes and corrective actions. Turboprop operation mirrors turbojet procedures but adds propeller considerations; pilots must monitor throttle/power lever settings, torquemeter pressure (which approximates total power output), and compute take‑off power to ensure exhaust gas temperature (EGT) and torquemeter pressure remain within limits for ambient conditions. 

Maintenance and testing procedures require adherence to manufacturer instructions. Calibration of turbine engines focuses on controlling EGT, engine cycles, and speed, as excessive EGT or speed shortens component life. The jetcal analyzer—a portable unit comprising thermocouples, rpm and EGT indicators, resistance and insulation checks, and supporting circuitry—is highlighted as a common tool for on‑site engine analysis. Turbine Engine Operation

The engine operating procedures presented here apply generally to turbofan, turboprop, turboshaft, and auxiliary power units (APU). The procedures, pressures, temperatures, and rpm that follow are intended primarily to serve as a guide. It should be understood that they do not have general application. The manufacturer's operating instructions should be consulted before attempting to start and operate any turbine engine.

A turbofan engine has only one power control lever. Adjusting the power lever, or throttle lever, sets up a thrust condition for which the fuel control meters fuel to the engine. Engines equipped with thrust reversers go into reverse thrust at throttle positions below idle. A separate fuel shutoff lever is usually provided on engines equipped with thrust reversers.

Prior to start, particular attention should be paid to the engine air inlet, the visual condition and free movement of the compressor and turbine assembly, and the parking ramp area fore and aft of the aircraft. The engine is started by using an external air power source, APU, or an already operating engine. Starter types and the engine starting cycle have been discussed previously. On multi-engine aircraft, the engines are usually started by an onboard APU that supplies the air pressure for a pneumatic starter on each engine. Air bled from the APU is used as a source of power for starting the engines.

During the start, it is necessary to monitor the tachometer, the oil pressure, and the exhaust gas temperature. The normal starting sequence is:

  1. Rotate the compressor with the starter;
  2. Turn the ignition on; and
  3. Open the engine fuel valve, either by moving the throttle to idle or by moving a fuel shutoff lever or turning a switch.

Adherence to the procedure prescribed for a particular engine is necessary as a safety measure and to avoid a hot or hung start. A successful start is noted first by a rise in exhaust gas temperature. If the engine does not light up, meaning that fuel starts to burn inside of the engine within a prescribed period of time, or if the exhaust gas starting temperature limit is exceeded, a hot start, the starting procedure should be aborted. Hot starts are not common, but when they do occur, they can usually be stopped in time to avoid excessive temperature by observing the exhaust gas temperature constantly during the start. When necessary, the engine is cleared of trapped fuel or gases by continuing to rotate the compressor with the starter, but with the ignition and fuel turned off. If the engine did not light off during start after the allotted time, about 10 seconds although this time varies from engine to engine, the fuel must be shut off as the engine is being filled with unburned fuel. A hung start is when the engine lights off, but the engine will not accelerate to idle rpm.

Ground Operation Engine Fire

Move the fuel shutoff lever to the off position if an engine fire occurs, or if the fire warning light is illuminated during the starting cycle. Continue cranking or motoring the engine until the fire has been expelled from the engine. If the fire persists, CO2 can be discharged into the inlet duct while it is being cranked. Do not discharge CO2 directly into the engine exhaust, because it may damage the engine. If the fire cannot be extinguished, secure all switches and leave the aircraft. If the fire is on the ground under the engine overboard drain, discharge the CO2 on the ground rather than on the engine. This also is true if the fire is at the tailpipe and the fuel is dripping to the ground and burning.

Engine Checks

Checking turbofan engines for proper operation consists primarily of simply reading the engine instruments and then comparing the observed values with those known to be correct for any given engine operating condition. After the engine has started, idle rpm has been attained, and the instrument readings have stabilized, the engine should be checked for satisfactory operation at idling speed. The oil pressure indicator, tachometer, and the exhaust gas temperature readings should be compared with the allowable ranges.

Checking Takeoff Thrust

Takeoff thrust is checked by adjusting the throttle to obtain a single, predicted reading on the engine pressure ratio indicator in the aircraft. The value for engine pressure ratio, which represents takeoff thrust for the prevailing ambient atmospheric conditions, is calculated from a takeoff thrust setting curve or, on newer aircraft, is a function of the onboard computer. This curve has been computed for static conditions. [Figure 10-74] Therefore, for all precise thrust checking, the aircraft should be stationary, and stable engine operation should be established. If it is needed for calculating thrust during an engine trim check, turbine discharge pressure (Pt7) is also shown on these curves. Appropriate manuals should be consulted for the charts for a specific make and model engine. Engine trimming procedure is also covered in Chapter 2, Engine Fuel & Fuel Metering Systems. summary.title: Turbine Engine Start, Monitoring, and Safety Procedures
summary.long_summary:
The passage outlines essential procedures for operating turbofan, turboprop, turboshaft, and APU turbine engines. Before start‑up, the air inlet, compressor and turbine condition, and surrounding area must be inspected. Engines are typically started using an external air source, an APU, or another running engine, with the starter rotating the compressor, ignition engaged, and fuel introduced. During start‑up, the tachometer, oil pressure, and exhaust gas temperature (EGT) must be continuously monitored. A successful start is indicated by a rise in EGT. If the engine fails to ignite within the prescribed time (≈10 seconds) or EGT exceeds limits (hot start), the start must be aborted, fuel shut off, and the compressor continued to rotate to clear unburned fuel. A hung start occurs when the engine lights but does not accelerate to idle rpm. 

In the event of a ground engine fire, the fuel shut‑off lever is moved to OFF, the engine is continued to be cranked, and CO₂ may be discharged into the inlet duct (never directly into the exhaust). If the fire persists, all switches are secured and the crew evacuates. 

Post‑start engine checks involve comparing instrument readings—oil pressure, tachometer, and EGT—to manufacturer‑specified limits at idle. Take‑off thrust verification is performed by setting the throttle to achieve the predicted engine pressure ratio (EPR) on the aircraft’s indicator, using take‑off thrust setting curves or onboard computer calculations. The aircraft must be stationary for accurate thrust checks, and turbine discharge pressure may also be referenced. All procedures emphasize adherence to the specific engine’s operating manual to ensure safety and prevent damage.

faqs.question: What is the purpose of the regulated pressure gauge in the differential compression tester?
faqs.answer: The regulated pressure gauge is used to set and monitor the test pressure (normally 80 psi) that is supplied to the cylinder while the compression test is being performed.

faqs.question: How do I set the regulated pressure to 80 psi before testing a cylinder?
faqs.answer: Open the shutoff valve, attach the air‑hose quick‑connect to the spark‑plug adapter, then turn the regulator knob on the tester until the regulated pressure gauge reads 80 psi while air is flowing into the cylinder.

faqs.question: How can I tell when the piston is at top dead center (TDC) during the test?
faqs.answer: When the piston reaches TDC the force required to turn the propeller decreases noticeably. If the propeller continues to move past TDC, the 15‑20 psi in the cylinder will push it forward, indicating you have passed TDC.

faqs.question: Why should I back the propeller up at least one blade before turning it forward again?
faqs.answer: Backing up eliminates backlash in the valve‑operating mechanism and ensures the piston rings stay seated on the lower ring lands before the next forward rotation.

faqs.question: What should I do if the cylinder‑pressure reading is below the engine’s minimum specified value?
faqs.answer: First, move the propeller in the direction of rotation to seat the piston rings, then re‑check all cylinders and record the readings. If compression remains low, run the engine to take‑off power and test again.

faqs.question: How can I determine whether low compression is caused by valve leakage or piston‑ring leakage?
faqs.answer: Listen for air escaping at the exhaust outlet (exhaust‑valve leak), at the air‑intake (intake‑valve leak), or from the engine case itself (piston‑ring leak) while the compression test is being performed.

faqs.question: What is the correct procedure for staking a valve if low compression persists after checking valve clearance?
faqs.answer: Place a fiber drift on the rocker arm over the valve stem and tap it several times with a 1‑2 lb hammer to dislodge any foreign material. After staking, rotate the engine with the starter or by hand to reseat the valve before re‑checking compression.

faqs.question: When is it acceptable to use the staking‑valve procedure?
faqs.answer: Only when the procedure is approved by the engine manufacturer; it should not be performed otherwise.

faqs.question: What safety precaution should I observe when closing the shutoff valve after the test?
faqs.answer: Make sure the propeller path is clear of all objects, because sufficient air pressure remains in the combustion chamber to rotate the propeller if the piston is not at TDC.

faqs.question: How do I interpret air‑leakage sounds to locate the source of compression loss?
faqs.answer: A hissing or blowing sound at the exhaust outlet indicates an exhaust‑valve leak; a similar sound at the air‑intake indicates an intake‑valve leak; and air escaping from the engine case suggests leakage past the piston rings.

summary.title: Differential Compression Tester Procedure and Troubleshooting
summary.long_summary:
The passage describes how to use a differential compression tester to measure and evaluate engine cylinder compression. First, set the regulated pressure gauge to 80 psi. Open the shutoff valve, attach the hose to the spark‑plug adapter, and manually turn the engine until the piston reaches top dead center (TDC) on the compression stroke, feeling a drop in propeller resistance. Close the shutoff valve and verify the regulated pressure remains at 80 psi; adjust the regulator if necessary. With the regulator set, read the cylinder pressure gauge; if the reading is below the engine’s minimum specification, rotate the propeller to seat the piston rings and repeat the test for all cylinders, recording results.

If any cylinder shows low compression, run the engine to take‑off power and retest. Persistent low compression warrants removal of the rocker‑box cover to check valve clearance. If clearance is adequate, insert a fiber drift over the valve stem and tap it with a light hammer to dislodge debris, then rotate the engine and re‑measure compression. This “staking” technique should only be performed with manufacturer approval.

For cylinders still below minimum compression, determine the leakage source: exhaust valve (listen at exhaust), intake valve (listen at intake), or piston rings (listen at the engine). Figures illustrate the tester setup and the two‑gauge unit. The procedure ensures accurate compression assessment and helps identify valve or ring problems.

Full authority digital engine controls (FADEC) (computer controls) also have means of checking the engine with the results displayed on the flight deck.

### Ambient Conditions

The sensitivity of gas turbine engines to compressor inlet air temperature and pressure necessitates that considerable care be taken to obtain correct values for the prevailing ambient air conditions when computing takeoff thrust. Some things to remember are:

1. The engine senses the air temperature and pressure at the compressor inlet. This is the actual air temperature just above the runway surface. When the aircraft is stationary, the pressure at the compressor inlet is the static field or true barometric pressure, and not the barometric pressure corrected to sea level that is normally reported by airport control towers as the altimeter setting. On FADEC engines, the computer reads this information and sends it to the engine controls.

2. Temperature sensed is the total air temperature (TAT) that is used by several onboard computers. The engine controls set the engine computers according to the TAT.

3. Relative humidity, which affects reciprocating engine power appreciably, has a negligible effect on turbine engine thrust, fuel flow, and rpm. Therefore, relative humidity is not usually considered when computing thrust for takeoff or determining fuel flow and rpm for routine operation.

### Engine Shutdown

On turbine engines that have a thrust reverser, retarding the aircraft throttle to idle or power lever to OFF cuts the fuel supply to the engine and shuts down the engine. On engines equipped with thrust reversers, this is accomplished by means of a separate fuel shutoff lever or switch. When an engine has been operated at high power levels for extended periods of time, a cool down time should be allowed before shutting down. It is recommended the engine be operated at below a low power setting, preferably at idle for a period of 5 minutes to prevent possible seizure of the rotors. summary.title: Compressor Blade Damage Types and Maintenance Terms
summary.long_summary:
Figure 10‑60 illustrates a progression of compressor blade damage, starting with a dent and calling, followed by a score, corrosion (pitting), and resulting cracks; other examples show scratches, burrs, burn damage, and a final repaired state (blend). Figure 10‑61 provides a glossary of blade‑maintenance terms. Each term is defined by its visual appearance and typical causes: 
- **Blend**: smooth repair of ragged edges to match surrounding contour. 
- **Bow**: blade bent, usually from foreign‑object impact. 
- **Burning**: discoloration or material flow caused by excessive heat. 
- **Burr**: ragged or turned‑out edge from grinding or cutting. 
- **Corrosion (pits)**: surface breakdown with a pitted look, due to moisture or other corrosive agents. 
- **Cracks**: partial fractures from shock, overload, defective material, or overheating. 
- **Dent**: small, smoothly rounded hollow from striking with a dull object. 
- **Gall**: metal transfer between surfaces caused by severe rubbing. 
- **Gouging**: material displacement resembling cutting or tearing, often from a large foreign body between moving parts. 
- **Growth**: blade elongation resulting from prolonged heat and centrifugal forces. 
- **Score**: deep scratches produced by chips between surfaces. 
- **Scratch**: narrow, shallow marks from sand, fine particles, or careless handling. 
Additional entries include **Pit** (synonymous with corrosion), **Profile** (blade contour), and **Gall**. The table links each damage type to its appearance and usual causes, providing a concise reference for inspection and maintenance of compressor blades.

summary.long_summary:
The passage describes the primary engine instrument gauges found in aircraft test cells and cockpits, focusing on fuel pressure, oil pressure, oil temperature, and fuel‑flow measurement. Fuel pressure is monitored at points such as the feed valve discharge nozzle, main supply line, carburetor, or fuel‑injection inlet. Gauges display a calibrated dial (0‑10 psi in the example) with a red line at 2 psi indicating the minimum allowable pressure, a green arc (2‑9 psi) showing the desired operating range, and a red line at 9 psi marking the maximum. Fuel‑injection systems require higher pressures, typically 10‑25 psi. 

Oil pressure is taken from the pressure side of the oil pump, usually with a single gauge per engine. The dial includes a red line at 25 psi (minimum), a green arc from 60‑85 psi (optimal range), and a red line at 100 psi (maximum). Low or absent pressure signals engine shutdown, while excessive needle oscillation suggests air in the lines or a malfunction. 

Oil temperature is measured at the oil inlet and outlet during run‑in. The gauge features a green arc indicating acceptable temperatures (25 °F up to just below 245 °F) and a red line at 245 °F as the maximum permissible temperature. 

Fuel‑flow meters quantify the fuel delivered to the engine. Three measurement methods are described: direct flow tubes with floats, pressure‑based flow gauges (common on light reciprocating engines), and turbine‑sensor transmitters used on turbine aircraft. The latter converts turbine speed into an electrical signal displayed as gallons per hour. In addition to the operations outlined previously, check the functioning of various items of aircraft equipment, such as generator systems, hydraulic systems, etc. ## Basic Engine Operating Principles ### Combustion Process Normal combustion occurs when the air-fuel mixture ignites in the cylinder and burns progressively at a fairly uniform rate across the combustion chamber. When ignition is properly timed, maximum pressure is built up just after the piston has passed top dead center at the end of the compression stroke. The flame fronts start at each spark plug and burn in more or less wavelike forms. [Figure 10-42] The velocity of the flame travel is influenced by the type of fuel, the ratio of the air-fuel mixture, and the pressure and temperature of the fuel mixture. With normal combustion, the flame travel is about 100 feet/second. The temperature and pressure within the cylinder rises at a normal rate as the air-fuel mixture burns. ### Detonation There is a limit, however, to the amount of compression and the degree of temperature rise that can be tolerated within an engine cylinder and still permit normal combustion. All fuels have critical limits of temperature and compression. Beyond this limit, they ignite spontaneously and burn with explosive violence. This instantaneous and explosive burning of the air-fuel mixture or, more accurately, of the latter portion of the charge is called detonation. Detonation is the spontaneous combustion of the unburned charge ahead of the flame fronts after ignition of the charge. [Figure 10-43] During normal combustion, the flame fronts progress from the point of ignition across the cylinder. These flame fronts compress the gases ahead of them. At the same time, the gases are being compressed by the upward movement of the piston. If the total compression on the remaining unburned gases exceeds the critical point, detonation occurs. The explosive burning during detonation results in an extremely rapid pressure rise. This rapid pressure rise and the high instantaneous temperature, combined with the high turbulence generated, cause a scrubbing action on the cylinder and the piston. This can burn a hole completely through the piston. The critical point of detonation varies with the ratio of fuel to air in the mixture. Therefore, the detonation characteristic of the mixture can be controlled by varying the air-fuel ratio. At high power output, combustion pressures and temperatures are higher than they are at low or medium power. Therefore, at high power, the air-fuel ratio is made richer than is needed for good combustion at medium or low power output. This is done because, in general, a rich mixture does not detonate as readily as a lean mixture.

summary.title: Opposed Engine Troubleshooting Guide
summary.long_summary:
The table outlines common problems for opposed‑type aircraft engines and provides probable causes with corrective actions. 

**Engine fails to start** – Causes include lack of fuel, under‑ or over‑priming, incorrect throttle setting, defective spark plugs or weak battery, magneto or breaker‑point issues, water in the carburetor, internal failures, and a magnetized impulse coupling. Remedies range from checking and refilling the fuel system, cleaning lines and valves, using proper priming procedures, opening the throttle and rotating the propeller, cleaning or replacing spark plugs, testing and replacing magneto wiring, draining water from the carburetor, checking internal timing, and demagnetizing the impulse coupling. 

**Engine fails to idle properly** – Possible reasons are frozen spark‑plug electrodes, idle‑cutoff mixture control, shorted ignition switch or loose ground, incorrect carburetor idle speed, wrong idle mixture, induction‑system leaks, low cylinder compression, faulty ignition system, open or leaking primer, and altitude‑incorrect spark‑plug settings. Solutions involve inspecting oil sump strainers, demagnetizing the impulse coupling, replacing or drying spark plugs, adjusting mixture and throttle settings, tightening connections, checking compression, and verifying the entire ignition system. 

**Low power and uneven running** – Typical causes are a dirty air filter, overly rich or lean mixture (indicated by sluggish operation, red exhaust, black smoke, overheating, or back‑firing), induction‑system leaks, defective spark plugs, improper fuel grade, malfunctioning magneto breaker points, faulty ignition wires or connectors, and incorrect valve clearance. Corrective steps include cleaning or replacing filters, adjusting carburetor mixture, checking and repairing primers, cleaning fuel lines, using the recommended fuel grade, tightening or replacing magneto and ignition components, adjusting valve clearance, and inspecting internal timing. 

The accompanying text explains that propeller load (power output) is directly proportional to engine speed. Engine power depends on manifold pressure, fuel flow, and RPM; throttle and RPM controls therefore govern power. In fixed‑pitch propeller installations, throttle alone controls both manifold pressure and RPM, allowing manifold pressure to serve as a proxy for power input and RPM for power output, provided other influencing factors are considered.

faqs.question: When should power‑input and power‑output measurements be used for comparing engine performance?
faqs.answer: Only for comparing an engine with its own previous performance or with identical powerplants; they are not suitable for comparing different types of engines.

faqs.question: How should the propeller be set for accurate engine performance checks?
faqs.answer: The blades must be against their low‑pitch stops (full low blade angle) so the blade angle is known and does not vary; the propeller control should be set to maximum or take‑off rpm, and checks are made at engine speeds below that setting.

faqs.question: How can manifold pressure readings indicate a potential engine problem?
faqs.answer: By comparing the manifold pressure required to reach a given rpm with the pressure recorded under known good conditions. A higher pressure for the same rpm (e.g., 32 inHg vs. 30 inHg at 2,200 rpm) suggests reduced power output, often due to a malfunctioning cylinder.

faqs.question: What are the main systems to inspect if an engine fault is suspected?
faqs.answer: 1) Ignition system, 2) Fuel‑metering system, 3) Induction system, 4) Power section (valves, cylinders, etc.), and 5) Instrumentation.

faqs.question: What information is useful for locating an engine malfunction?
faqs.answer: Details such as any roughness noted and its conditions, engine and spark‑plug time‑on‑engine, results of ignition‑system and power checks, when the trouble first appeared, presence of back‑firing or after‑firing, and whether full‑throttle performance was normal.

faqs.question: What are common causes of back‑firing in an engine?
faqs.answer: 1) Valves holding open or sticking open, 2) Lean mixture, 3) Intake pipe leakage, and 4) Incorrect valve adjustment that gives one cylinder too small or too large a charge.

faqs.question: How can ignition‑system problems lead to back‑firing, and how do they differ from basic magneto failures?
faqs.answer: Cracked distributor blocks or high‑tension leaks between ignition leads can cause the charge to ignite during the intake stroke, producing back‑fire. These problems are usually not in the basic magneto itself; a magneto failure would prevent the engine from running or cause it to cut out at high speeds, whereas replacing a cracked distributor (part of the magneto) can correct the back‑firing.

faqs.question: How can an engine’s performance be compared to previous records or other engines?
faqs.answer: By keeping adequate performance records (manifold pressure vs. rpm under similar atmospheric conditions) and then comparing current readings to those past values or to readings from identical engines on the same or similar aircraft.

faqs.question: What steps help determine whether a problem lies in the fuel‑metering or ignition system?
faqs.answer: First identify which phase—fuel metering or ignition—is involved by observing symptoms (e.g., back‑firing, low power, roughness). Then isolate the faulty cylinder or system using the recorded information (manifold pressure, rpm, roughness conditions, etc.) to pinpoint whether the issue is in the fuel delivery, the ignition leads/distributor, or another component.

Engine condition can be assessed by comparing relative measures of power input (manifold pressure) and power output (rpm) under consistent atmospheric conditions. Atmospheric pressure and air temperature must be accounted for because they affect air density. For accurate comparison, the propeller should be set to its low‑pitch stop (maximum or take‑off rpm) so blade angle remains constant; the propeller governor then maintains a constant rpm regardless of power input.

A practical example: an engine that now requires 32 in‑Hg manifold pressure to reach 2,200 rpm, whereas it previously needed only 30 in‑Hg under the same conditions, indicates a loss of performance, often pointing to a malfunctioning cylinder. Engine performance can be benchmarked against its own historical data, against identical engines on the same aircraft, or against other aircraft with the same installation, provided records are kept.

When a fault is suspected, the likely systems are: ignition, fuel‑metering, induction, power section (valves, cylinders), or instrumentation. Systematic questioning—such as noting roughness, engine time, spark‑plug condition, ignition check results, onset timing, back‑firing, and full‑throttle performance—helps isolate the problem.

Back‑firing or low power usually stems from either the fuel‑metering or ignition system, and may involve a single cylinder. Common causes include stuck valves, lean mixture, intake leaks, incorrect valve adjustment, cracked distributor blocks, or high‑tension leaks. Magneto failures typically prevent the engine from running altogether, whereas a cracked distributor can cause ignition during the intake stroke. Identifying the faulty subsystem enables targeted repair and rapid restoration of engine performance.

### Valve Blow-By

Valve blow-by is indicated by a hissing or whistle when pulling the propeller through prior to starting the engine, when turning the engine with the starter, or when running and blow-by past the intake valve is audible through the carburetor.

Correct valve blow-by immediately to prevent valve failure and possible engine failure by taking the following steps:

1. Perform a cylinder compression test to locate the faulty cylinder.
2. Check the valve clearance on the affected cylinder. If the valve clearance is incorrect, the valve may be sticking in the valve guide. To release the sticking valve, place a fiber drift on the rocker arm immediately over the valve stem and strike the drift several times with a mallet. Sufficient hand pressure should be exerted on the fiber drift to remove any space between the rocker arm and the valve stem prior to hitting the drift.
3. If the valve is not sticking and the valve clearance is incorrect, adjust it as necessary.
4. Determine whether blow-by has been eliminated by again pulling the engine through by hand or turning it with the starter. If blow-by is still present, it may be necessary to replace the cylinder.

### Cylinder Compression Tests

The cylinder compression test determines if the valves, piston rings, and pistons are adequately sealing the combustion chamber. If pressure leakage is excessive, the cylinder cannot develop its full power. The purpose of testing cylinder compression is to determine whether cylinder replacement is necessary. The detection and replacement of defective cylinders prevents a complete engine change because of cylinder failure. It is essential that cylinder compression tests be made periodically. Low compression, for the most part, can be traced to leaky valves.

Conditions that affect engine compression are:

1. Incorrect valve clearances.
2. Worn, scuffed, or damaged piston.
3. Excessive wear of piston rings and cylinder walls.
4. Burned or warped valves.
5. Carbon particles between the face and the seat of the valve or valves.

6. Early or late valve timing.

Perform a compression test as soon as possible after the engine is shut down so that piston rings, cylinder walls, and other parts are still freshly lubricated. However, it is not necessary to operate the engine prior to accomplishing compression tests during engine buildup or on individually replaced cylinders. In such cases, before making the test, spray a small quantity of lubricating oil into the cylinder(s), and turn the engine over several times to seal the piston and rings in the cylinder barrel.

Be sure that the ignition switch is in the OFF position so that there is no accidental firing of the engine. Remove necessary cowling and the most accessible spark plug from each cylinder. When removing the spark plugs, identify them to coincide with the cylinder. Close examination of the plugs aid in diagnosing problems within the cylinder. Records of previous compression checks help in determining progressive wear conditions and in establishing the necessary maintenance actions.

### Differential Pressure Tester

The differential pressure tester checks the compression of aircraft engines by measuring the leakage through the cylinders. The design of this compression tester is such that minute valve leakages can be detected, making possible the replacement of cylinders where valve burning is starting. The operation of the compression tester is based on the principle that, for any given airflow through a fixed orifice, a constant pressure drop across the orifice results.

As the airflow and pressure changes, pressure varies accordingly in the same direction. If air is supplied under pressure to the cylinder with both intake and exhaust valves closed, the amount of air that leaks by the valves or piston rings indicates their condition; the perfect cylinder would have no leakage. The differential pressure tester requires the application of air pressure to the cylinder being tested with the piston at top-center compression stroke. [Figure 10-53]

Guidelines for performing a differential compression test are:

1. Perform the compression test as soon as possible after engine shutdown to provide uniform lubrication of cylinder walls and rings.
2. Remove the most accessible spark plug from the cylinder, or cylinders, and install a spark plug adapter in the spark plug insert.
3. Connect the compression tester assembly to a 100 to 150 psi compressed air supply. [Figure 10-54] With the shutoff valve on the compression tester closed,

faqs.question: What is valve blow‑by and how can I tell if it is occurring?
faqs.answer: Valve blow‑by is indicated by a hissing or whistling sound when you pull the propeller through by hand before starting the engine, when you turn the engine with the starter, or when the engine is running and the blow‑by past the intake valve can be heard through the carburetor.

faqs.question: What steps should I follow to correct valve blow‑by?
faqs.answer: 1) Perform a cylinder compression test to locate the faulty cylinder. 2) Check the valve clearance on that cylinder; if it is incorrect, the valve may be sticking. 3) To release a sticking valve, place a fiber drift on the rocker arm over the valve stem, apply hand pressure, and strike the drift several times with a mallet. 4) If the valve is not sticking but the clearance is wrong, adjust the clearance as required. 5) Re‑test for blow‑by by pulling the engine through by hand or turning it with the starter. If blow‑by persists, the cylinder may need to be replaced.

faqs.question: How do I perform a cylinder compression test on an aircraft engine?
faqs.answer: Perform the test as soon as possible after the engine is shut down. Ensure the ignition switch is OFF. Remove the most accessible spark plug from each cylinder, noting which plug belongs to which cylinder. If the cylinder has been idle for a while, spray a small amount of lubricating oil into it and turn the engine several times to seat the rings. Then attach the compression tester and record the pressure readings. Keep records of each test to track wear over time.

faqs.question: What are the most common causes of low compression in an aircraft engine?
faqs.answer: Low compression is usually caused by one or more of the following: incorrect valve clearances, worn, scuffed or damaged pistons, excessive wear of piston rings or cylinder walls, burned or warped valves, carbon deposits between the valve face and seat, and early or late valve timing.

faqs.question: Why is it important to conduct compression tests periodically?
faqs.answer: Periodic compression tests help detect defective cylinders early, allowing replacement of only the faulty cylinder instead of a complete engine change. Early detection prevents loss of power, reduces wear, and ensures safe engine operation.

faqs.question: How can I release a valve that is sticking in its guide?
faqs.answer: Place a fiber drift on the rocker arm directly over the valve stem, apply firm hand pressure to eliminate any gap between the rocker arm and the stem, and then strike the drift several times with a mallet. This should free the sticking valve.

faqs.question: What is a differential pressure tester and what does it measure?
faqs.answer: A differential pressure tester checks aircraft engine compression by measuring the amount of air that leaks through the cylinders when both intake and exhaust valves are closed. It detects minute valve leakages, allowing early identification of cylinders with beginning valve burn.

faqs.question: What air pressure should be used with a differential pressure tester?
faqs.answer: Connect the tester to a compressed‑air source delivering between 100 and 150 psi.

faqs.question: What are the guidelines for performing a differential compression test?
faqs.answer: 1) Perform the test as soon as possible after engine shutdown to keep cylinder walls and rings uniformly lubricated. 2) Remove the most accessible spark plug (or plugs) and install a spark‑plug adapter in the plug socket. 3) Connect the tester assembly to a 100‑150 psi air supply, keeping the tester’s shut‑off valve closed until you are ready to begin the test.

faqs.question: How do I ensure I am testing the correct cylinder when removing spark plugs?
faqs.answer: Identify each spark plug as you remove it so it matches the cylinder it came from. Keeping a record of which plug belongs to which cylinder helps diagnose problems and track compression results over time.

summary.title: Valve Blow‑By Diagnosis and Cylinder Compression Testing
summary.long_summary:
The text outlines how to identify and correct valve blow‑by in aircraft engines and explains the role of cylinder compression testing. Blow‑by is heard as a hissing or whistling sound when the propeller is pulled by hand, when the starter turns the engine, or during operation, indicating leakage past the intake valve. To remedy it, first perform a cylinder compression test to locate the faulty cylinder. Then inspect valve clearance; if the valve sticks, a fiber drift is placed on the rocker arm over the valve stem and struck with a mallet while applying hand pressure to free it. If clearance is merely incorrect, adjust it. Re‑test for blow‑by; persistent leakage may require cylinder replacement.

Compression testing evaluates the sealing ability of valves, piston rings, and pistons. Low compression often stems from leaky valves, incorrect clearances, worn pistons or rings, warped valves, carbon deposits, or improper timing. Tests should be done immediately after shutdown while parts are still lubricated; a small amount of oil may be sprayed into the cylinder and the engine turned to seal rings. Spark plugs are removed, identified, and examined for diagnostic clues, with records kept for trend analysis.

A differential pressure tester measures leakage by applying 100‑150 psi air to a cylinder with both valves closed at top‑dead‑center. The pressure drop across a fixed orifice indicates minute valve leaks, allowing early detection of valve burning. Guidelines include performing the test promptly after shutdown, using a spark‑plug adapter, and ensuring the tester’s shut‑off valve is closed before connection.

faqs.question: Why does the power unit fail to turn over when I try to start the engine?
faqs.answer: The most common causes are no air reaching the starter or the propeller brake being locked. Check the starter air valve solenoid and the air supply, and unlock the brake by turning the propeller by hand in the normal rotation direction.

faqs.question: What can cause the power unit to fail to start even though the starter turns?
faqs.answer: Possible reasons include low starter speed due to inadequate air supply, a fuel selector valve that is inoperative or locked OFF, an inoperative fuel pump, a dirty aircraft fuel filter, or a closed fuel‑control cutoff valve.

faqs.question: How should I remedy a power‑unit start failure caused by fuel‑system problems?
faqs.answer: Check the starter air valve solenoid and air supply, verify the power supply to electrically operated valves and replace any defective valves, inspect the fuel pump for sheared drives or internal damage and check for air leaks at the outlet, clean or replace the fuel filter, and ensure the fuel‑control actuator is being energized; replace the actuator or control if necessary.

faqs.question: My engine fires but will not accelerate to the correct speed. What might be wrong?
faqs.answer: Potential causes are insufficient fuel supply to the control unit, a sticking fuel‑control main‑metering valve, a sticking fuel‑control bypass valve, a drain valve stuck open, or a starting‑fuel enrichment pressure switch set too high.

faqs.question: What steps should I take if the engine’s acceleration temperature is too high during start?
faqs.answer: The likely causes are a bypass valve stuck closed, an incorrectly adjusted acceleration cam, a defective fuel nozzle, or a fuel‑control thermostat failure. Remedy by flushing the system and replacing the control, adjusting or replacing the cam, installing a known good nozzle, or replacing the control (thermostat).

faqs.question: Why is the acceleration temperature during start too low, and how can I fix it?
faqs.answer: A low acceleration temperature is usually due to an incorrectly adjusted acceleration cam on the fuel control. Replace the control to correct the adjustment.

faqs.question: After start‑up the engine speed keeps cycling. What does this indicate?
faqs.answer: Unstable operation of the fuel‑control governor can cause speed cycling. The recommended remedy is to continue running the engine so the control can condition itself.

faqs.question: What should I do if the power‑unit oil pressure drops severely?
faqs.answer: Check the oil supply and refill if necessary. Also verify that the oil‑pressure transmitter or indicator is functioning correctly; repair or replace it if it is giving false readings.

faqs.question: How can I address oil leakage at the accessory‑drive seals?
faqs.answer: The leakage is caused by seal failure. Replace the faulty seal(s).

faqs.question: The engine cannot reach its maximum controlled speed of 100 %. What are the possible causes and fixes?
faqs.answer: Possible causes are a faulty propeller governor or a faulty fuel control/air‑sensing tip. Replace the propeller control assembly, and replace the faulty fuel control. If the control is dirty, clean it by passing air pressure in the reverse direction of normal flow through the internal engine passage and sensing tip.

summary.title: Turboprop Engine Troubleshooting Guide
summary.long_summary:
The table lists typical turboprop engine problems, their most likely causes, and recommended corrective actions. 
1. **Power unit does not turn over** – May be due to lack of starter air or a locked propeller brake. Check the starter‑air valve solenoid, verify air supply, and manually rotate the propeller to free the brake. 
2. **Power unit fails to start** – Possible low starter‑air flow, inoperative fuel selector valve, faulty fuel pump, dirty fuel filter, or closed fuel‑control cutoff valve. Inspect the air valve solenoid, power supply, and electrically operated valves; test the pump for damage and leaks; clean or replace the filter; ensure the actuator receives power. 
3. **Engine fires but will not accelerate** – Insufficient fuel to the control unit, sticking metering or bypass valves, or a stuck drain valve/high pressure‑switch setting. Verify all fuel valves are open and pumps work, flush the system and replace the control or drain valve as needed. 
4. **High acceleration temperature on start** – Stuck bypass valve, incorrectly set acceleration cam, defective nozzle, or thermostat failure. Flush and replace the control, adjust or replace the cam, replace the nozzle, or replace the control if the thermostat is bad. 
5. **Low acceleration temperature** – Incorrectly adjusted acceleration cam; replace the control. 
6. **Engine speed cycles after start** – Unstable fuel‑control governor; allow the engine to run so the governor can condition itself. 
7. **Severe oil‑pressure drop** – Low oil supply or faulty pressure transmitter/indicator; refill oil and repair or replace the sensor. 
8. **Oil leak at accessory drive seals** – Seal failure; replace the seal(s). 
9. **Unable to reach 100 % max speed** – Faulty propeller governor or fuel control/air‑sensing tip; replace the propeller control assembly or the fuel control, cleaning the sensing tip if dirty. 
10. **High vibration indication** – Possible pickup or meter malfunction; calibrate the meter, run the engine gradually, and if vibration persists, consider overhaul after confirming the meter is functional. 
Overall, the guide emphasizes systematic inspection of air, fuel, oil, and control systems, followed by cleaning, adjustment, or replacement of defective components.

faqs.question: Why is it important to ground the jetcal analyzer when using an AC power supply?

faqs.question: What type of probes should be used for heating during engine testing?
faqs.answer: Only heater probes that are specifically designed for use on the engine should be employed.

faqs.question: What are the probable causes of engine rumble during starting and low‑power cruise conditions?
faqs.answer: The possible causes are a pressurizing and drain valve malfunction, a cracked air duct, or a fuel control malfunction.

faqs.question: What actions should be taken if the engine rpm hangs up during starting?
faqs.answer: If the hang‑up is due to low ambient temperature, try turning on the fuel booster pump or moving the start lever to the run position earlier in the cycle. Otherwise, inspect the compressor and turbine sections for damage.

faqs.question: What can cause high oil temperature in a turbojet engine and how should it be addressed?
faqs.answer: High oil temperature may be caused by a scavenge pump failure or a fuel heater malfunction. Check the lubricating system and scavenge pumps, and replace the fuel heater if it is faulty.

faqs.question: What are the likely reasons for high oil consumption and what checks are recommended?
faqs.answer: High oil consumption can result from scavenge pump failure, high sump pressure, or gearbox seal leakage. Check the scavenge pumps, verify sump pressure according to the manufacturer's maintenance manual, and test the gearbox seal by pressurizing the overboard vent.

faqs.question: What might cause overboard oil loss and how can it be diagnosed?
faqs.answer: Overboard oil loss can be caused by high airflow through the tank, foaming oil, or excessive oil return through the vent system. Diagnose by checking the oil for foaming, performing a vacuum check of the sumps, and inspecting the scavenge pumps.

faqs.question: What functions can most engine analyzers perform for aircraft EGT system testing?
faqs.answer: Most analyzers can functionally check the EGT system for errors without running the engine, test individual thermocouples and parallel harnesses for continuity and accuracy, measure EGT circuit resistance and insulation, determine engine rpm accuracy, and establish the proper relationship between EGT and engine rpm during run‑up.

faqs.question: How should thermocouples be checked before they are placed in a parallel harness?
faqs.answer: Thermocouples should be individually checked for continuity and then tested in the parallel harness for continuity, accuracy, and proper resistance before engine run‑up.

faqs.question: Why must a voltmeter not be used to check the potentiometer for continuity?
faqs.answer: Using a voltmeter on the potentiometer can damage the galvanometer and the standard battery cell, so a voltmeter should never be used for this purpose.
