Compressor Section

Maintenance of the compressor, or cold section, is one of concern because damage to blades can cause engine failure. Much of the damage to the blades arises from foreign matter being drawn into the turbine engine air intakes. The atmosphere near the ground is filled with tiny particles of dirt, oil, soot, and other foreign matter. A large volume of air is introduced into the compressor, and centrifugal force throws the dirt particles outward so that they build up to form a coating on the casing, the vanes, and the compressor blades. Accumulation of dirt on the compressor blades reduces the aerodynamic efficiency of the blades with resultant deterioration in engine performance. The efficiency of the blades is impaired by dirt deposits in a manner similar to that of an aircraft wing under icing conditions. Unsatisfactory acceleration and high exhaust gas temperature can result from foreign deposits on compressor components.

An end result of foreign particles, if allowed to accumulate in sufficient quantity, would be inefficiency. The condition can be remedied by periodic inspection, cleaning, and repair of compressor components.

Inspection & Cleaning

Minor damage to axial-flow engine compressor blades may be repaired if the damage can be removed without exceeding the allowable limits established by the manufacturer. Typical compressor blade repair limits are shown in Figure 10-57. Well-rounded damage to leading and trailing edges that is evident on the opposite side of the blade is usually acceptable without re-work, provided the damage is in the outer half of the blade only, and the indentation does not exceed values specified in the engine manufacturer's service and overhaul instruction manuals. When working on the inner half of the blade, damage must be treated with extreme caution. Repaired compressor blades are inspected by either magnetic particle or fluorescent penetrant inspection methods to ensure that all traces of the damage have been removed. All repairs must be well blended so that surfaces are smooth. [Figure 10-58] No cracks of any extent are tolerated in any area.

Whenever possible, stoning and local re-work of the blade should be performed parallel to the length of the blade. Re-work must be accomplished by hand, using stones, files, or emery cloth. Do not use a power tool to buff the entire area of the blade. The surface finish in the repaired area must be comparable to that of a new blade. On centrifugal flow engines, it is difficult to inspect the compressor inducers without first removing the air-inlet screen. After removing the screen, clean the compressor inducer and inspect it with a strong light. Check each vane for cracks by slowly turning the compressor. Look for cracks in the leading edges. A crack is usually cause for component rejection. The compressor inducers are normally the parts that are damaged by the impingement of foreign material during engine operation.

Compressor inducers are repaired by stoning out and blending the nicks and dents in the critical band (1½ to 2½ inches from the outside edge), if the depth of such nicks or dents does not exceed that specified in the engine manufacturer's service or overhaul instruction manuals. Repair nicks by stoning out material beyond the depth of damage to remove the resulting cold-worked metal. A generous radius must be applied at the edges of the blend. After blending the nick, it should be smoothed over with a crocus cloth. Pitting nicks or corrosion found on the sides of the inducer vanes are similarly removed by blending.

Causes of Blade Damage

Loose objects often enter an engine either accidentally or through carelessness. Foreign object damage (FOD), such as pencils, tools, and flashlights, are often drawn into the engine and can cause damage to the fan blades. [Figure 10-59] Do not carry any objects in pockets when working around operational turbine engines.

A compressor rotor can be damaged beyond repair by tools that are left in the air intake, where they are drawn into the engine on subsequent starts. A simple solution to the problem is to check the tools against a tool checklist. Prior to starting a turbine engine, make a minute inspection of engine inlet ducts to assure that items, such as nuts, bolts, lock wire, or tools, were not left there after work had been performed.

Figure 10-60 shows some examples of blade damage to an axial-flow engine. The descriptions and possible causes of blade damage are given in Figure 10-61. Corrosion pitting is not considered serious on the compressor stator vanes of axial-flow engines if the pitting is within the allowed tolerance. Do not attempt to repair any vane by straightening, brazing, welding, or soldering. Crocus cloth, fine files, and stones are used to blend out damage by removing a minimum of material and leaving a surface finish comparable to that of a new part. The purpose of this blending is to minimize stresses that concentrate at dents, scratches, or cracks.

The inspection and repair of air intake guide vanes, swirl vanes, and screens on centrifugal-flow engines necessitates the use of a strong light. Inspect screen assemblies for breaks, rips, or holes. Screens may be tin-dipped to tighten the wire mesh, provided the wires are not worn too thin. If the frame strip or lugs have separated from the screen frames, re-brazing may be necessary.

sentiment.summary: The compressor section requires regular inspection, cleaning, and careful repair to prevent blade damage from foreign particles and ensure engine efficiency.

faqs.question: Why is regular inspection and cleaning of compressor blades important?
faqs.answer: Because dirt, oil, soot and other foreign particles can build up on the blades, reducing their aerodynamic efficiency, causing poor acceleration and high exhaust gas temperatures, and eventually leading to engine inefficiency or failure.

faqs.question: How does foreign matter affect compressor blade performance?
faqs.answer: Foreign particles are thrown outward by centrifugal force and coat the casing, vanes, and blades. The coating acts like ice on an aircraft wing, decreasing aerodynamic efficiency and degrading overall engine performance.

faqs.question: What are the acceptable limits for repairing minor damage on compressor blades?
faqs.answer: Minor, well‑rounded damage on the outer half of a blade may be repaired if the indentation does not exceed the values specified in the engine manufacturer’s service and overhaul manuals. Damage on the inner half must be treated with extreme caution and must stay within the same manufacturer‑defined limits.

faqs.question: Which inspection methods are used to verify repaired compressor blades?
faqs.answer: Repaired blades are examined with magnetic‑particle inspection or fluorescent‑penetrant inspection to ensure that all traces of damage have been removed and that no cracks remain.

faqs.question: What tools and techniques should be used for reworking damaged compressor blades?
faqs.answer: Re‑work must be done by hand using stones, files, or emery cloth; power tools are not permitted. The repaired surface must be blended smoothly and finished to a quality comparable to a new blade.

faqs.question: How are compressor inducer blades inspected and repaired on centrifugal‑flow engines?
faqs.answer: The air‑inlet screen is first removed, the inducer is cleaned, and a strong light is used to examine each vane while slowly turning the compressor. Cracks lead to rejection. Nicks or dents in the critical band (1½–2½ inches from the outer edge) are stoned out, blended with a generous radius, and then smoothed with crocus cloth, provided the depth is within manufacturer limits.

faqs.question: What common sources cause foreign object damage (FOD) to compressor blades?
faqs.answer: Objects such as pencils, tools, flashlights, nuts, bolts, lock wire, or any loose items that are accidentally left in engine inlet ducts can be drawn into the engine and strike the fan or compressor blades.

faqs.question: What steps should be taken before starting a turbine engine to prevent tool‑related damage?
faqs.answer: Use a tool checklist, perform a minute inspection of the engine inlet ducts, and verify that no tools, nuts, bolts, or other objects remain in the air‑intake area before start‑up.

faqs.question: Why is it prohibited to repair compressor vanes by brazing, welding, or soldering?
faqs.answer: These processes can introduce stresses and material inconsistencies; the approved method is to blend out damage with crocus cloth, fine files, and stones, removing only the minimum material needed to achieve a surface finish comparable to a new part.

faqs.question: How should air‑intake guide vanes, swirl vanes, and screens be inspected on centrifugal‑flow engines?
faqs.answer: Inspect them with a strong light for breaks, rips, holes, or looseness. Screens may be tin‑dipped to tighten the mesh if the wires are not overly thin, and any separated frame strips or lugs may require re‑brazing.

summary.title: Compressor Blade Maintenance, Inspection, and Repair Guidelines
summary.long_summary:
The compressor (cold) section of a turbine engine is vulnerable to blade damage caused by foreign particles such as dirt, oil, soot, and debris drawn in through the air intake. These contaminants accumulate on casings, vanes, and blades, reducing aerodynamic efficiency much like ice on an aircraft wing, leading to poor acceleration and high exhaust gas temperatures. Regular inspection, cleaning, and repair are essential to maintain performance.

Minor blade damage can be repaired if it stays within manufacturer‑specified limits. Acceptable damage includes well‑rounded dents on the outer half of the blade that do not exceed prescribed depths; inner‑half damage requires extreme caution. After repair, blades must be examined with magnetic‑particle or fluorescent‑penetrant methods to confirm complete removal of defects, and no cracks are tolerated. Repairs should be performed by hand using stones, files, or emery cloth, avoiding power tools, and the finished surface must match that of a new blade.

Compressor inducers on centrifugal‑flow engines are inspected after removing the inlet screen, using strong lighting and slow rotation to detect cracks, especially on leading edges. Repairs involve stoning and blending nicks within the critical band, followed by smoothing with crocus cloth. Pitting or corrosion within allowable tolerances is acceptable, but straightening, brazing, welding, or soldering of vanes is prohibited.

Foreign‑object damage (FOD) from tools, nuts, bolts, or other loose items is a major risk; a tool checklist and pre‑start inlet inspection are required to prevent such incidents. Screens, guide vanes, and swirl vanes must also be inspected for breaks, wear, or looseness, with tin‑dipping or re‑brazing used when necessary. Overall, diligent inspection, proper cleaning, and careful hand‑crafted repairs ensure compressor reliability and engine safety.

topics.context:
Visual Inspection

Visual inspection should precede all other inspection procedures. Parts should not be cleaned before a preliminary visual inspection, since indications of a failure may often be detected from the residual deposits of metallic particles in some recesses in the engine.

Several terms are used to describe defects detected in engine parts during inspection. Some of the more common terms and definitions are:

  1. Abrasion—an area of roughened scratches or marks usually caused by foreign matter between moving parts or surfaces.
  2. Brinelling—one or more indentations on bearing races, usually caused by high static loads or application of force during installation or removal. Indentations are rounded or spherical due to the impression left by the contacting balls or rollers of the bearing.
  3. Burning—surface damage due to excessive heat. It is usually caused by improper fit, defective lubrication, or over-temperature operation.
  4. Burnishing—polishing of one surface by sliding contact with a smooth, harder surface. Usually no displacement nor removal of metal.
  5. Chafing—a condition caused by a rubbing action between two parts under light pressure that results in wear.
  6. Chipping—breaking away of pieces of material, that is usually caused by excessive stress concentration or careless handling.
  7. Corrosion—loss of metal by a chemical or electrochemical action. The corrosion products are easily removed by mechanical means. Iron rust is an example of corrosion.
  8. Crack—a partial separation of material usually caused by vibration, overloading, internal stresses, defective assembly, or fatigue. Depth may be a few thousandths, to the full thickness of the piece.
  9. Cut—loss of metal, usually to an appreciable depth over a relatively long and narrow area, by mechanical means, as would occur with the use of a saw blade, chisel, or sharp-edged stone striking a glancing blow.
  10. Dent—a small, rounded depression in a surface usually caused by the part being struck with a rounded object.
  11. Erosion—loss of metal from the surface by mechanical action of foreign objects, such as grit or fine sand. The eroded area is rough and may be lined in the direction that the foreign material moved relative to the surface.
  12. Flaking—the breaking loose of small pieces of metal or coated surfaces, that is usually caused by defective plating or excessive loading.
  13. Fretting—a condition of surface erosion caused by minute movement between two parts usually clamped together with considerable unit pressure.
  14. Galling—a severe condition of chafing or fretting in which a transfer of metal from one part to another occurs. It is usually caused by a slight movement of mated parts having limited relative motion and under high loads.
  15. Gouging—a furrowing condition in which a displacement of metal has occurred (a torn effect). It is usually caused by a piece of metal, or foreign material, between close moving parts.
  16. Grooving—a recess, or channel, with rounded and smooth edges usually caused by faulty alignment of parts.
  17. Inclusion—presence of foreign or extraneous material entirely within a portion of metal. Such material is introduced during the manufacture of rod, bar, or tubing by rolling or forging.
  18. Nick—a sharp-sided gouge or depression with a V-shaped bottom, that is generally the result of careless handling of tools and parts.
  19. Peening—a series of blunt depressions in a surface.
  20. Pick up or scuffing—a buildup or rolling of metal from one area to another, that is usually caused by insufficient lubrication, clearances, or foreign matter.
  21. Pitting—small hollows of irregular shape in the surface, usually caused by corrosion or minute mechanical chipping of surfaces.
  22. Scoring—a series of deep scratches caused by foreign particles between moving parts or careless assembly or disassembly techniques.
  23. Scratches—shallow, thin lines or marks, varying in degree of depth and width, caused by presence of fine foreign particles during operation or contact with other parts during handling.
  24. Stain—a change in color, locally, causing a noticeably different appearance from the surrounding area.
  25. Upsetting—a displacement of material beyond the normal contour or surface (a local bulge or bump). Usually indicates no metal loss.

Examine all gears for evidence of pitting or excessive wear.

faqs.question: Why should visual inspection be performed before cleaning engine parts?
faqs.answer: Because indications of a failure may often be detected from the residual deposits of metallic particles in some recesses, which could be removed if the parts were cleaned first.

faqs.question: What is brinelling and what causes it?
faqs.answer: Brinelling is one or more indentations on bearing races, usually caused by high static loads or the application of force during installation or removal. The indentations are rounded or spherical from the impression left by the bearing balls or rollers.

faqs.question: How does burning differ from burnishing?
faqs.answer: Burning is surface damage due to excessive heat, often caused by improper fit, defective lubrication, or over‑temperature operation. Burnishing is a polishing of one surface by sliding contact with a smoother, harder surface and usually involves no displacement or removal of metal.

faqs.question: What is fretting and how is it different from galling?
faqs.answer: Fretting is a condition of surface erosion caused by minute movement between two parts that are clamped together with considerable pressure. Galling is a more severe form of chafing or fretting where metal is transferred from one part to another, typically occurring with slight relative motion under high loads.

faqs.question: What causes pitting on a surface and how can it be recognized?
faqs.answer: Pitting consists of small hollows of irregular shape on the surface, usually caused by corrosion or minute mechanical chipping. It appears as tiny depressions in the material.

faqs.question: What does the term ‘upsetting’ mean in the context of visual inspection?
faqs.answer: Upsetting is a displacement of material beyond the normal contour or surface, creating a local bulge or bump, and usually indicates no metal loss.

faqs.question: What should be examined on all gears during visual inspection?
faqs.answer: All gears should be examined for evidence of pitting or excessive wear.

faqs.question: How is corrosion defined and can it be removed?
faqs.answer: Corrosion is the loss of metal by a chemical or electrochemical action. The corrosion products are easily removed by mechanical means; iron rust is an example.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a crack and a chip?
faqs.answer: A crack is a partial separation of material, often caused by vibration, overloading, internal stresses, defective assembly, or fatigue, and can range from a few thousandths to the full thickness of the piece. A chip is a breaking away of pieces of material, usually caused by excessive stress concentration or careless handling.

faqs.question: What does ‘scoring’ refer to in defect terminology?
faqs.answer: Scoring is a series of deep scratches caused by foreign particles between moving parts or by careless assembly or disassembly techniques.

summary.title: Visual Inspection and Defect Terminology for Engine Parts
summary.long_summary: The document emphasizes that visual inspection must be performed before any other inspection method and before cleaning, because residual metallic deposits can reveal failures. It provides a comprehensive glossary of defect terms commonly observed on engine components, defining each condition and its typical cause. The list includes abrasion, brinelling, burning, burnishing, chafing, chipping, corrosion, crack, cut, dent, erosion, flaking, fretting, galling, gouging, grooving, inclusion, nick, peening, pick‑up/scuffing, pitting, scoring, scratches, stain, and upsetting. Each definition describes the appearance of the defect and the mechanisms that produce it, such as foreign particles, high static loads, improper fit, lubrication issues, vibration, overloading, or manufacturing inclusions. The text concludes with a specific instruction to examine all gears for signs of pitting or excessive wear, reinforcing the importance of detecting these defects early to prevent further damage.

faqs.question: What are the critical areas of the valve that need inspection?

faqs.question: Can minor pitting on the valve face be repaired?

faqs.answer: Use a valve spring compression tester to compress the spring until its total height matches the manufacturer’s specification. The dial on the tester will indicate the pressure, in pounds, required to achieve that compression.

summary.title: Valve Inspection Guidelines and Measurement Tolerances
summary.long_summary: The valve face must run true with the stem within a 0.0015‑inch tolerance. Figure 10‑12 shows where to measure runout and the edge‑thickness section (location A). When measuring thickness, the valve face itself is excluded. Critical areas—face and tip (Figure 10‑13)—must be inspected for pitting and excessive wear; minor pitting can be removed by grinding. Stretch and wear are evaluated with a micrometer or a valve radius gauge (Figure 10‑14). Using a micrometer, stretch appears as a reduced stem diameter near the neck; the stem diameter and guide fit should be recorded. Visual inspection for physical damage, burning, or corrosion is required; damaged valves must not be reused. Spring compression is tested with a valve spring compression tester (Figure 10‑15); the spring is compressed to the manufacturer‑specified height and the dial reading indicates the required pressure in pounds. These steps ensure valve integrity and proper operation.

  1. Do not leave heater probe assemblies in the exhaust nozzle during engine run-up.
  2. Never allow the heater probes to go over 900 °C (1,652 °F). Exceeding these temperatures results in damage to the jetcal analyzer and heater probe assemblies.

Continuity Check of Aircraft EGT Circuit

To eliminate any error caused by one or more inoperative aircraft thermocouples, a continuity check is performed. The check is made by heating one heater probe to between 500 and 700 °C and placing the hot probe over each of the aircraft thermocouples, one at a time. The EGT indicator must show a temperature rise as each thermocouple is checked. When large numbers (eight or more) of thermocouples are used in the harness, it is difficult to see a rise on the aircraft instrument because of the electrical characteristics of a parallel circuit. Therefore, the temperature indication of the aircraft thermocouples is read on the potentiometer of the analyzer by using the check cable and necessary adapter.

Functional Check of Aircraft EGT Circuit

During the EGT system functional test and the thermocouple harness checks, the analyzer has a specific degree of accuracy at the test temperature, which is usually the maximum operating temperature of the turbine engine. [Figure 10-78] Each engine has its own maximum operating temperature, that can be found in applicable technical instructions.

The test is made by heating the engine thermocouples in the exhaust nozzle or turbine section to the engine test temperature. The heat is supplied by heater probes through the necessary cables. With the engine thermocouples hot, their temperature is registered on the aircraft EGT indicator. At the same time, the thermocouples embedded in the heater probes, which are completely isolated from the aircraft system, are picking up and registering the same temperature on the test analyzer.

The temperature registered on the aircraft EGT indicator should be within the specified tolerance of the aircraft system and the temperature reading on the temperature analyzer. When the temperature difference exceeds the allowable tolerance, troubleshoot the aircraft system.

summary.title: Jetcal Analyzer EGT Circuit Inspection and Testing Procedures
summary.long_summary:
The Jetcal analyzer instrument compartment (Figure 10‑77) contains switches, receptacles, a potentiometer, rheostat, fuses and other controls used for testing aircraft exhaust gas temperature (EGT) circuits. Each aircraft type uses a specially designed heater probe; probes must not be altered or left in the exhaust nozzle, and temperatures must never exceed 900 °C (1,652 °F) to avoid damage. 

**Continuity Check** – To verify that aircraft thermocouples are functional, a heater probe is heated to 500‑700 °C and placed sequentially over each thermocouple. The EGT indicator should show a temperature rise for each probe. When many thermocouples are in parallel, the rise may be hard to see on the aircraft gauge; instead the analyzer’s potentiometer is read via a check cable and adapter. 

**Functional Check** – The analyzer’s accuracy is confirmed at the engine’s maximum operating temperature (Figure 10‑78). Heater probes heat the engine‑mounted thermocouples in the exhaust or turbine section to this test temperature. The aircraft EGT indicator and the analyzer’s isolated thermocouples should display the same temperature within the specified tolerance. If the difference exceeds the allowable limit, the aircraft EGT system must be troubleshooted. 

These procedures ensure reliable EGT measurements, protect the analyzer and heater probes from overheating, and provide a systematic method for verifying continuity and functional performance of aircraft thermocouple circuits.

topics.context:
Piston, Valve Train, & Piston Pin

When applicable, check for flatness of the piston head using a straightedge and thickness gauge. [Figure 10-2] If a depression is found, check for cracks on the inside of the piston. A depression in the top of the piston usually means that detonation has occurred within the cylinder.

Inspect the exterior of the piston for scores and scratches. Scores on the top ring land are not cause for rejection, unless they are excessively deep. Deep scores on the side of the piston are usually a reason for rejection.

Examine the piston for cracked skirts, broken ring lands, and scored piston-pin holes. Do not mistake casting marks or laps for a crack. During major overhaul, most pistons are generally replaced, as it requires more labor to clean and inspect the piston than it costs to replace it.

Crankshaft & Connecting Rods

Carefully inspect all surfaces of the crankshaft for cracks. Check the bearing surfaces for evidence of galling, scoring, or other damage. When a shaft is equipped with oil transfer tubes, check them for tightness.

Visual inspection of connecting rods should be done with the aid of a magnifying glass or bench microscope. A rod that is obviously bent or twisted should be rejected without further inspection. Inspect all surfaces of the connecting rods for cracks, corrosion, pitting, galling, or other damage. Galling is caused by a slight amount of movement between the surfaces of the bearing insert and the connecting rod during periods of high loading, such as that produced during over-speed or excessive manifold pressure operation. The visual evidence produced by galling appears as if particles from one contacting surface had welded to the other. Evidence of any galling is sufficient reason for rejecting the complete rod assembly. Galling is a distortion in the metal and is comparable to corrosion in the manner in which it weakens the metallic structure of the connecting rod.

Cleaning

After visually inspecting engine recesses for deposits of metal particles, it is important to clean all engine parts thoroughly to facilitate further inspection. Two processes for cleaning engine parts are:

  1. Degreasing to remove dirt and sludge (soft carbon).
  2. The removal of hard carbon deposits by decarbonizing, brushing or scraping, and grit-blasting.

Degreasing

Degreasing can be done by immersing or spraying the part in a suitable commercial solvent. [Figure 10-3] Extreme care must be used if any water-mixed degreasing solutions containing caustic compounds or soap are used. Such compounds, in addition to being potentially corrosive to aluminum and magnesium, may become impregnated in the pores of the metal and cause oil foaming when the engine is returned to service. Therefore, when using water-mixed solutions, it is imperative that the parts be rinsed thoroughly and completely in clear boiling water after degreasing. Regardless of the method and type of solution used, coat or spray all parts with lubricating oil immediately after cleaning to prevent corrosion.

Removing Hard Carbon

While the degreasing solution removes dirt, grease, and soft carbon, deposits of hard carbon almost invariably remain on many interior surfaces. To remove these deposits, they must first be loosened by immersion in a tank containing a decarbonizing solution (usually heated). A great variety of commercial decarbonizing agents are available. Decarbonizers, like the degreasing solutions previously mentioned, fall generally into two categories, water-soluble and hydrocarbons. The same caution concerning the use of water-soluble degreasers is applicable to water-soluble decarbonizers.

Caution: When using a decarbonizing solution on magnesium castings, avoid immersing steel and magnesium parts in the same decarbonizing tank, as this practice often results in damage to the magnesium parts from corrosion.

Decarbonizing will usually loosen most of the hard carbon deposits remaining after degreasing. However, the complete removal of all hard carbon generally requires brushing, scraping, or grit-blasting. In all of these operations, be careful to avoid damaging the machined surfaces. In particular, wire brushes and metal scrapers must never be used on any bearing or contact surface.

faqs.question: When are scores on a piston considered a reason for rejection?
faqs.answer: Scores on the top ring land are acceptable unless they are excessively deep. Deep scores on the side of the piston are usually a reason for rejection.

faqs.question: What should I look for to differentiate a crack from a casting mark on a piston?
faqs.answer: Cracks appear as sharp, continuous breaks, while casting marks or laps are surface irregularities that do not extend through the metal. Do not mistake casting marks for cracks.

faqs.question: Why are pistons usually replaced during a major overhaul instead of cleaned and inspected?
faqs.answer: Cleaning and inspecting a piston requires more labor than the cost of a new piston, so most pistons are replaced during a major overhaul.

faqs.question: What are the key inspection points for a crankshaft?
faqs.answer: Inspect all crankshaft surfaces for cracks, check bearing surfaces for galling, scoring, or other damage, and verify that any oil‑transfer tubes are tight.

faqs.question: How should I inspect connecting rods for damage, and what findings require rejection?
faqs.answer: Use a magnifying glass or bench microscope to examine all rod surfaces for cracks, corrosion, pitting, galling, or other damage. A rod that is visibly bent or twisted must be rejected without further inspection.

faqs.question: What is galling on a connecting rod, and why does it lead to rejection?
faqs.answer: Galling is a distortion caused by slight movement between the bearing insert and the rod under high load, appearing as welded‑together particles. Any evidence of galling weakens the rod and is sufficient reason to reject the entire rod assembly.

faqs.question: What are the two main cleaning processes for engine parts and their purposes?
faqs.answer: 1) Degreasing – removes dirt, sludge, and soft carbon. 2) Removal of hard carbon – uses decarbonizing solutions, followed by brushing, scraping, or grit‑blasting to eliminate hard carbon deposits.

faqs.question: What precautions must be taken when using water‑mixed degreasing solutions?
faqs.answer: Water‑mixed solutions containing caustic compounds or soap can corrode aluminum and magnesium and become trapped in metal pores, causing oil foaming. After degreasing, parts must be rinsed thoroughly in clear boiling water and then coated with lubricating oil immediately.

faqs.question: How should hard carbon be removed, and what safety measures are required when decarbonizing magnesium parts?
faqs.answer: First, immerse parts in a heated decarbonizing solution (water‑soluble or hydrocarbon). Then, complete removal may require brushing, scraping, or grit‑blasting—avoiding damage to machined surfaces and never using wire brushes or metal scrapers on bearing or contact surfaces. When decarbonizing magnesium castings, do not place steel and magnesium parts in the same tank to prevent corrosion of the magnesium.

summary.title: Engine Component Inspection and Cleaning Procedures
summary.long_summary:
The document outlines inspection and cleaning methods for major engine components. For pistons, inspectors should verify head flatness with a straightedge and thickness gauge; depressions suggest detonation and require internal crack checks. Exterior scores are acceptable unless excessively deep, especially on side walls. Cracked skirts, broken ring lands, and scored pin holes warrant rejection, while casting marks are not considered cracks. During major overhauls, pistons are usually replaced because cleaning and inspection are labor‑intensive.

Crankshaft inspection involves a thorough visual check for cracks and damage on bearing surfaces, including galling or scoring, and verification of oil transfer tube tightness. Connecting rods must be examined under magnification; any bent or twisted rod is rejected outright. Inspectors look for cracks, corrosion, pitting, and galling—metal distortion resembling welded particles that weakens the rod and mandates rejection of the entire assembly.

Cleaning procedures begin with a visual survey for metal particles, followed by degreasing to eliminate dirt, sludge, and soft carbon. Degreasing may be done by immersion or spray with commercial solvents; water‑mixed solutions containing caustics or soaps must be rinsed thoroughly in boiling water to prevent corrosion and oil foaming, especially on aluminum or magnesium parts. After cleaning, all parts should be coated with lubricating oil.

Hard carbon removal requires a decarbonizing solution, typically heated, with similar water‑soluble or hydrocarbon classifications as degreasers. Caution is advised when cleaning magnesium castings; steel and magnesium should not share the same tank to avoid corrosion. Decarbonizing loosens most hard carbon, but complete removal often needs brushing, scraping, or grit‑blasting—avoiding wire brushes or metal scrapers on bearing or contact surfaces. Manufacturer recommendations should be followed for grit‑blasting procedures.

This section must be thoroughly inspected along with the inspection the combustion section and turbine section of the engine. Inspect the exhaust cone and exhaust nozzle for cracks, warping, buckling, or hot spots. Hot spots on the tail cone are a good indication of a malfunctioning fuel nozzle or combustion chamber. The inspection and repair procedures for the hot section of any one gas turbine engine share similarities to those of other gas turbine engines. One usual difference is the nomenclature applied to the various parts of the hot section by the different manufacturers. Other differences include the manner of disassembly, the tooling necessary, and the repair methods and limits. ### Engine Ratings The flat rating of a turbine engine is the thrust performance that is guaranteed by the manufacturer for a new engine under specific operating conditions, such as takeoff, maximum continuous climb, and cruise power settings. The turbine inlet temperature is proportional to the energy available to turn the turbine. This means that the hotter the gases are that are entering the turbine section of the engine, the more power is available to turn the turbine wheel. The exhaust temperature is proportional to the turbine inlet temperature. Regardless of how or where the exhaust temperature is taken on the engine for the flight deck reading, this temperature is proportional to the temperature of the exhaust gases entering the first stage of inlet guide vanes. A higher EGT corresponds to a larger amount of energy to the turbine so it can turn the compressor faster. This works fine until the temperature reaches a point when the turbine inlet guide vanes start to be damaged. EGT must be held constant or lowered as the result of a prolonged hot section life and, at the same time, provide the thrust to meet the certification requirements. Before high bypass turbofan engines, some older types of engines used water injection to increase thrust for takeoff (wet). This is the maximum allowable thrust for takeoff. The rating is obtained by actuating the water-injection system and setting the computed wet thrust with the throttle, in terms of a predetermined turbine discharge pressure or engine pressure ratio for the prevailing ambient conditions. The rating is restricted to takeoff, is time-limited, and has an altitude limitation. Water injection is not used very much on turbine engines any more.

It is instrumented by total pressure pickups in the engine inlet (Pt2) and in the turbine exhaust (Pt7). The reading is displayed in the flight deck by the EPR gauge, which is used in making engine power settings. [Figure 10-72]

faqs.question: Which parts of the exhaust section need to be inspected for heat cracking?
faqs.answer: The exhaust cone and exhaust nozzle should be inspected for cracks, warping, buckling, or hot spots.

faqs.question: What does a hot spot on the tail cone indicate?
faqs.answer: A hot spot on the tail cone is a good indication of a malfunctioning fuel nozzle or combustion chamber.

faqs.question: Do inspection and repair procedures differ between gas turbine engine manufacturers?
faqs.answer: The overall procedures are similar, but differences exist in the nomenclature used for hot‑section parts, the manner of disassembly, the tooling required, and the specific repair methods and limits.

faqs.question: What is a flat rating for a turbine engine?
faqs.answer: A flat rating is the thrust performance guaranteed by the manufacturer for a new engine under specific operating conditions such as take‑off, maximum continuous climb, and cruise power settings.

faqs.question: How does turbine inlet temperature affect engine power?
faqs.answer: Turbine inlet temperature is proportional to the energy available to turn the turbine; hotter gases entering the turbine provide more power to turn the turbine wheel, which raises the exhaust gas temperature (EGT) and thrust.

faqs.question: Why must EGT be held constant or lowered during operation?
faqs.answer: Because excessive EGT can damage the turbine inlet guide vanes; maintaining or lowering EGT protects the hot section while still providing the thrust required to meet certification requirements.

faqs.question: What is water injection and why is it rarely used on modern turbine engines?
faqs.answer: Water injection (wet thrust) was used on some older engines to increase take‑off thrust by injecting water into the combustion stream. It is time‑limited, altitude‑restricted, and now seldom used because newer engine designs achieve required thrust without it.

faqs.question: How is the wet thrust rating determined and what are its limitations?
faqs.answer: The rating is obtained by actuating the water‑injection system and setting the computed wet thrust with the throttle, based on a predetermined turbine discharge pressure or engine pressure ratio for the prevailing ambient conditions. It is limited to take‑off, has a time limit, and an altitude limitation.

faqs.question: What clearances are measured on a turbine engine and how?
faqs.answer: Clearances measured include the tip clearance between turbine blades and the shroud, and the clearance between the turbine wheel and the exhaust cone. These are measured with a suitable measuring tool, as illustrated in Figures 10‑70 and 10‑71.

faqs.question: What does the Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR) indicate and how is it measured?
faqs.answer: EPR indicates the thrust being developed by a turbofan engine and is used to set power for take‑off. It is measured by total‑pressure pickups in the engine inlet (Pt2) and in the turbine exhaust (Pt7) and displayed on the flight‑deck EPR gauge.

summary.title: Turbine Engine Exhaust Inspection, Ratings, and Instrumentation Overview
summary.long_summary:
The exhaust section of a turbine engine is prone to heat‑induced cracking and must be inspected together with the combustion and turbine sections. Inspectors should check the exhaust cone and nozzle for cracks, warping, buckling, and hot spots, the latter often indicating a faulty fuel nozzle or combustion chamber. While hot‑section inspection and repair procedures are similar across gas‑turbine models, differences exist in part nomenclature, disassembly methods, required tooling, and repair limits.

Engine flat ratings define the guaranteed thrust under specific conditions such as take‑off, climb, and cruise. Turbine inlet temperature (TIT) directly affects the energy available to spin the turbine; higher exhaust gas temperature (EGT) means more power but also raises the risk of damaging turbine inlet guide vanes. Consequently, EGT must be managed to balance turbine life with thrust requirements.

Historically, some older high‑bypass turbofans used water injection to boost take‑off thrust (wet thrust). This method raises turbine discharge pressure for a limited time and altitude, but it is now rarely employed.

Maintenance includes precise clearance measurements: tip clearance between turbine blades and shroud, and clearance between the turbine wheel and exhaust cone, as illustrated in Figures 10‑70 and 10‑71.

Engine pressure ratio (EPR) is a primary instrument for setting thrust on many turbofan aircraft. It is derived from total pressure sensors at the engine inlet (Pt2) and turbine exhaust (Pt7) and displayed on the flight‑deck gauge, guiding power settings during take‑off and other phases of flight.

topics.context:
Therefore, any leaning out gives a mixture that is leaner than best power. ### Idle Mixture The idle mixture curve shows how the mixture changes when the idle mixture adjustment is changed. [Figure 10-48] Note that the greatest effect is at idling speeds. However, there is some effect on the mixture at airflows above idling. The airflow at which the idle adjustment effect cancels out varies from minimum cruise to maximum cruise. The exact point depends on the type of carburetor and the carburetor setting. In general, the idle adjustment affects the air-fuel mixture up to low cruise on engines equipped with float-type carburetors. This means that incorrect idle mixture adjustments can easily give faulty cruise performance, as well as poor idling. There are variations in mixture requirements between one engine and another because of the fuel distribution within the engine and the ability of the engine to cool. Remember, a carburetor setting must be rich enough to supply a combustible mixture for the leanest cylinder. If fuel distribution is poor, the overall mixture must be richer than would be required for the same engine if distribution were good. The engine's ability to cool depends on such factors as cylinder design (including the design of the cooling fins), compression ratio, accessories on the front of the engine that cause individual cylinders to run hot, and the design of the baffling used to deflect airflow around the cylinder. At takeoff power, the mixture must be rich enough to supply sufficient fuel to keep the hottest cylinder cool. ### Induction Manifold The induction manifold provides the means of distributing air, or the air-fuel mixture, to the cylinders. Whether the manifold handles an air-fuel mixture or air alone depends on the type of fuel metering system used. On an engine equipped with a carburetor, the induction manifold distributes an air-fuel mixture from the carburetor to the cylinders. On a fuel-injection engine, the fuel is delivered to injection nozzles, one in each cylinder, that provide the proper spray pattern for efficient burning. Thus, the mixing of fuel and air takes place at the inlet port to the cylinder. On a fuel-injection engine the induction manifold handles only air. The induction manifold is an important item because of the effect it can have on the air-fuel mixture that finally reaches the cylinder. Fuel is introduced into the airstream by the carburetor in a liquid form. To become combustible, the fuel must be vaporized in the air. This vaporization takes place in the induction manifold, which includes the internal supercharger, if one is used. Any fuel that does not vaporize clings to the walls of the intake pipes. Obviously, this affects the effective air-fuel ratio of the mixture that finally reaches the cylinder in vapor form. This explains the reason for the apparently rich mixture required to start a cold engine. In a cold engine, some of the fuel in the airstream condenses out and clings to the walls of the manifold. This is in addition to that fuel that never vaporized in the first place. As the engine warms up, less fuel is required because less fuel is condensed out of the airstream and more of the fuel is vaporized, thus giving the cylinder the required air-fuel mixture for normal combustion. Any leak in the induction system has an effect on the mixture reaching the cylinders. This is particularly true of a leak at the cylinder end of an intake pipe. At manifold pressures below atmospheric pressure, such a leak leans out the mixture. This occurs because additional air is drawn in from the atmosphere at the leaky point. The affected cylinder may overheat, fire intermittently, or even cut out altogether. ### Operational Effect of Valve Clearance While considering the operational effect of valve clearance, keep in mind that all aircraft reciprocating engines of current design use valve overlap. Valve overlap is when the intake and exhaust valves are open at the same time. This takes advantage of the momentum of the entering and exiting gases to improve the efficiency of getting air-fuel in and exhaust gases out. Figure 10-49 shows the pressures at the intake and exhaust ports under two different sets of operating conditions. In one case, the engine is operating at a manifold pressure of 35 "Hg. Barometric pressure (exhaust back pressure) is 29 "Hg. This gives a pressure acting in the direction indicated by the arrow of differential of 6 "Hg (3 psi). During the valve overlap period, this pressure differential forces the air-fuel mixture across the combustion chamber toward the open exhaust. This flow of air-fuel mixture forces ahead of it the exhaust gases remaining in the cylinder, resulting in complete scavenging of the combustion chamber.

faqs.question: What effect does adjusting the idle mixture have on engine performance?
faqs.answer: Changing the idle mixture adjustment mainly alters the air‑fuel ratio at idle speeds, but it also influences the mixture at low cruise airflow; an incorrect setting can cause poor idling and faulty cruise performance.

faqs.question: At what airflow range does the idle mixture adjustment have the most impact?
faqs.answer: The greatest effect of the idle mixture adjustment occurs at idle airflow, with a diminishing effect as airflow increases toward low cruise; the point where the effect cancels out varies between minimum and maximum cruise depending on the carburetor type and setting.

faqs.question: How does a faulty idle mixture adjustment affect cruise performance?
faqs.answer: If the idle mixture is set incorrectly, the mixture can remain too rich or too lean into low‑cruise conditions, leading to reduced cruise power, higher fuel consumption, or unstable engine operation.

faqs.question: Why must a carburetor setting be rich enough for the leanest cylinder?
faqs.answer: The carburetor must provide a mixture that is rich enough to keep the cylinder that receives the least fuel (the leanest cylinder) combustible; otherwise that cylinder could run too lean, overheat, or misfire.

faqs.question: How do fuel distribution and engine cooling influence mixture requirements?
faqs.answer: Poor fuel distribution forces the overall mixture to be richer than otherwise needed, while the engine’s cooling ability—affected by cylinder design, compression ratio, front accessories, and baffling—determines how rich the mixture must be to keep the hottest cylinder cool, especially at take‑off power.

faqs.question: What role does the induction manifold play in a carbureted engine versus a fuel‑injection engine?
faqs.answer: In a carbureted engine the induction manifold carries the air‑fuel mixture from the carburetor to the cylinders; in a fuel‑injection engine it carries only air, because fuel is injected directly into each cylinder’s inlet port.

faqs.question: Why is a richer mixture needed when starting a cold engine?
faqs.answer: When the engine is cold, some fuel in the airstream condenses on the walls of the induction manifold and does not vaporize, so a richer mixture is required to ensure enough vaporized fuel reaches the cylinders for combustion.

faqs.question: How does a leak in the induction system affect the air‑fuel mixture and engine operation?
faqs.answer: A leak, especially near the cylinder end of an intake pipe, allows extra atmospheric air to enter when manifold pressure is below atmospheric, leaning out the mixture; this can cause the affected cylinder to overheat, fire intermittently, or shut down.

faqs.question: What is valve overlap and how does it improve engine efficiency?
faqs.answer: Valve overlap is the period when both intake and exhaust valves are open simultaneously; the momentum of the entering fresh charge and exiting exhaust gases creates a pressure differential that pushes the air‑fuel mixture across the combustion chamber, aiding complete scavenging and improving efficiency.

faqs.question: How does the pressure differential during valve overlap affect scavenging of the combustion chamber?
faqs.answer: During overlap, the higher pressure on the intake side relative to the exhaust side forces the air‑fuel mixture toward the open exhaust, pushing remaining exhaust gases ahead of it and achieving thorough scavenging of the chamber.

summary.title: Idle Mixture, Induction Manifold, and Valve Overlap Impacts
summary.long_summary:
The idle mixture adjustment primarily influences the air‑fuel ratio at idle speeds, but its effect can extend into low‑cruise conditions, especially on float‑type carburetors. An incorrect idle setting may cause poor idle quality and degraded cruise performance. Mixture requirements vary between engines due to differences in fuel distribution and cooling ability; a carburetor must be set rich enough to satisfy the leanest cylinder, and poor fuel distribution demands a richer overall mixture. Cooling depends on cylinder design, compression ratio, front‑mounted accessories, and baffling, with the hottest cylinder requiring a richer mixture at take‑off power.

The induction manifold distributes air—or the air‑fuel mixture—to the cylinders. In carbureted engines it carries a premixed charge; in fuel‑injected engines it carries only air, with fuel injected directly at each cylinder inlet. Vaporization of fuel occurs within the manifold; any fuel that fails to vaporize adheres to the walls, effectively leaning the mixture that reaches the cylinder. This explains why cold engines need a richer mixture: more fuel condenses on the cold walls. As the engine warms, less fuel condenses and more vaporizes, reducing the required mixture richness.

Leaks in the induction system, particularly near the cylinder end of an intake pipe, introduce extra atmospheric air when manifold pressure is below atmospheric, leaning the mixture. The affected cylinder may overheat, misfire, or shut down.

Regarding valve clearance, modern aircraft reciprocating engines employ valve overlap, where intake and exhaust valves are open simultaneously. The pressure differential created during overlap (e.g., 6 in‑Hg or 3 psi at a manifold pressure of 35 in‑Hg versus exhaust back pressure of 29 in‑Hg) forces the fresh air‑fuel mixture into the cylinder, pushing remaining exhaust gases out and achieving complete scavenging. This overlap improves cylinder filling efficiency and overall engine performance.

Piston Repairs

Piston repairs are not required as often as cylinder repairs since most of the wear is between the piston ring and cylinder wall, valve stem and guide, and valve face and seat. A lesser amount of wear is encountered between the piston skirt and cylinder, ring and ring groove, or piston pin and bosses.

The most common repair is the removal of scores. Usually, these may be removed only on the piston skirt if they are very light. On engines where the entire rotating and reciprocating assembly is balanced, the pistons must weigh within one-fourth ounce of each other. When a new piston is installed, it must be within the same weight tolerance as the one removed. It is not enough to have the pistons matched alone; they must be matched to the crankshaft, connecting rods, piston pins, etc. To make weight adjustments on new pistons, the manufacturer provides a heavy section at the base of the skirt. To decrease weight, file metal evenly off the inside of this heavy section. The piston weight can be decreased easily, but welding, metalizing, or plating cannot be done to increase the piston weight.

If ring grooves are worn or stepped, the pistons are normally replaced. Small nicks on the edge of the piston pin boss may be sanded down. Deep scores inside the boss, or anywhere around the boss, are definite reasons for rejection. It has become more economical to replace pistons rather than reconditioning and reusing old ones, especially during overhaul.

Cylinder Grinding & Honing

If a cylinder has excessive taper, out-of-roundness, step, or its maximum size is beyond limits, it can be reground to the next allowable oversize. If the cylinder walls are lightly rusted, scored, or pitted, the damage may be removed by honing or lapping.

faqs.question: How should the valve be ground against the stone to avoid overheating?
faqs.answer: Turn on the machine and grinding fluid, then push the valve lightly against the stone and swing it back and forth, making sure the valve stem does not swing off either edge of the stone and that plenty of grinding fluid covers the tip.

faqs.question: What is the purpose of the 45° V‑way when restoring the valve bevel?
faqs.answer: The V‑way, set at approximately 45°, holds the valve while you twist the tip onto the stone; grinding with a light touch around the tip restores the bevel that prevents scratching the valve guide when the valve is installed.

faqs.question: What steps are involved in lapping a valve to the seat?
faqs.answer: Apply a small amount of lapping compound to the valve face, insert the valve into the guide, rotate it with a lapping tool until a smooth, gray finish appears at the contact area, then remove all compound from the valve face, seat, and surrounding areas.

faqs.question: How is a valve leak test performed after lapping?
faqs.answer: Install the valve in the cylinder, hold the valve stem with your fingers, pour kerosene or solvent into the valve port, keep finger pressure on the stem, and watch for any kerosene leaking past the valve into the combustion chamber. If no leak is seen, the valve is properly seated.

faqs.question: What should be done if kerosene leaks past the valve during the leak test?
faqs.answer: Continue the lapping operation until the leakage stops, then repeat the leak test to confirm a proper seal.

faqs.question: What are the common causes of improper valve and seat grinding indicated by incorrect leak test results?
faqs.answer: Incorrect indications (shown in Figure 10‑29) arise from issues such as an uneven bevel, insufficient lapping compound removal, or improper grinding angles, which can be diagnosed and corrected by adjusting the grinding or lapping procedures.

faqs.question: How are piston weight adjustments made on new pistons?
faqs.answer: The manufacturer provides a heavy section at the base of the piston skirt; to decrease weight, file metal evenly off the inside of this heavy section. Weight can be decreased easily, but increasing weight requires replacing the piston because welding, metalizing, or plating are not permitted.

faqs.question: What weight tolerance must pistons meet in a balanced engine?
faqs.answer: All pistons must weigh within one‑fourth ounce of each other and must match the weight tolerance of the crankshaft, connecting rods, piston pins, and other rotating components.

faqs.question: When should pistons be replaced rather than repaired?
faqs.answer: Pistons are typically replaced if ring grooves are worn or stepped, if there are deep scores inside the piston pin boss, or if any damage makes reconditioning uneconomical; small, light scores on the piston skirt may be removed, but deeper damage warrants replacement.

faqs.question: What are the options for repairing a cylinder that has excessive taper, out‑of‑roundness, or a step beyond limits?
faqs.answer: The cylinder can be reground to the next allowable oversize, or if the walls are lightly rusted, scored, or pitted, the damage may be removed by honing or lapping. Regrinding is a specialized job usually performed by a powerplant mechanic.

summary.title: Valve Grinding, Lapping, and Engine Component Repair Procedures
summary.long_summary:
The passage outlines step‑by‑step methods for restoring engine valves, pistons, and cylinders. Valve work begins by clamping the valve beside a grinding stone, applying abundant grinding fluid, and lightly swinging the valve tip against the stone without allowing the stem to leave the stone’s edges. Overheating is avoided by continuous fluid coverage. If grinding removes the bevel on the valve tip, a 45° V‑way is mounted, the valve is held in it, and the tip is gently ground around to re‑establish the bevel that protects the valve guide.

After grinding, the valve may need lapping to the seat. A small amount of lapping compound is placed on the valve face, the valve is inserted into its guide, and rotated with a lapping tool until a uniform gray band appears, indicating proper contact. All compound must then be removed. Leak testing follows: the valve is installed in the cylinder, the stem held manually, and kerosene or solvent poured into the valve port. If no fluid leaks into the combustion chamber, the valve is correctly seated; otherwise, further lapping is required. Figures illustrate a correctly lapped valve and the grinding setup.

The text also covers piston repairs, noting that most wear occurs between rings and cylinder walls, valve stems and guides, and valve faces and seats. Light scores on piston skirts may be removed; pistons must be weight‑matched within a quarter‑ounce tolerance, with weight reduced by filing a heavy base section. Ring‑groove wear typically mandates piston replacement, and deep boss scores are grounds for rejection.

Finally, cylinder grinding and honing are described. Excessive taper, out‑of‑roundness, or oversize cylinders can be reground to the next allowable size, while light rust, scoring, or pitting can be remedied by honing or lapping. Regrinding is a specialized task generally beyond the routine power‑plant mechanic’s scope.

Generally, standard aircraft cylinder oversizes are 0.010 inch, 0.015 inches, 0.020 inch, or 0.030 inch. Aircraft cylinders have relatively thin walls and may have a nitrided surface, that must not be ground away. Nitriding is a surface hardening process that hardens the steel surface to a depth of several thousandths of an inch. Any one manufacturer usually does not allow all of the above oversizes. Some manufacturers do not allow regrinding to an oversize at all. The manufacturer's overhaul manual, or parts catalog, usually lists the oversizes allowed for a particular make and model engine.

To determine the regrind size, the standard bore size must be known. This usually can be determined from the manufacturer's specifications or manuals. The regrind size is figured from the standard bore. For example, a certain cylinder has a standard bore of 3.875 inches. To have a cylinder ground to 0.015 inches oversize, it is necessary to grind to a bore diameter of 3.890 inch (3.875 + 0.015). A tolerance of ±0.0005 inches is usually accepted for cylinder grinding.

Another factor to consider when determining the size to which a cylinder must be regrind is the maximum wear that has occurred. If there are spots in the cylinder wall that are worn larger than the first oversize, then obviously it is necessary to grind to the next oversize to clean up the entire cylinder.

The type of finish desired in the cylinder is an important consideration when ordering a regrind. Some engine manufacturers specify a fairly rough finish on the cylinder walls, that allows the rings to seat even if they are not lapped to the cylinder. Other manufacturers desire a smooth finish to which a lapped ring seats without much change in ring or cylinder dimensions. The latter type of finish is more expensive to produce.

The standard used when measuring the finish of a cylinder wall is known as micro-inch root mean square (micro-inch RMS). In a finish where the depth of the grinding scratches are one-millionth (0.000001) of an inch deep, it is specified as 1 micro-inch RMS. Most aircraft cylinders are ground to a finish of 15 to 20 micro-inch RMS. Several low-powered engines have cylinders that are ground to a relatively rough 20- to 30-micro-inch RMS finish. On the other end of the scale, some manufacturers require a superfinish of approximately 4- to 6-micro-inch RMS.

Cylinder grinding is accomplished by a firmly mounted stone that revolves around the cylinder bore, as well as up and down the length of the cylinder barrel. [Figure 10-30] The cylinder, the stone, or both may move to get this relative movement. The size of the grind is determined by the distance the stone is set away from the centerline of the cylinder. Some cylinder bore grinding machines produce a perfectly straight bore, while others are designed to grind a choked bore. A choked bore grind refers to the manufacturing process in which the cylinder walls arc ground to produce a smaller internal diameter at the top than at the bottom. The purpose of this type grind or taper is to maintain a straight cylinder wall during operation. As a cylinder heats up during operation, the head and top of the cylinder are subjected to more heat than the bottom. This causes greater expansion at the top than at the bottom, thereby maintaining the desired straight wall.

After grinding a cylinder, it may be necessary to hone the cylinder bore to produce the desired finish. In this case, specify the cylinder regrind size to allow for some metal removal during honing. The usual allowance for honing is 0.001 inch. If a final cylinder bore size of 3.890 inches is desired, specify the regrind size of 3.889 inches, and then hone to 3.890 inches.

There are several different makes and models of cylinder hones. The burnishing hone is used only to produce the desired finish on the cylinder wall. The more elaborate

faqs.question: How can a mechanic tell when an aircraft cylinder needs to be re‑ground?
faqs.answer: The mechanic must look for signs such as excessive wear, out‑of‑tolerance bore size, or poor valve‑seat contact (e.g., fuzzy edges, too‑narrow contact, or too‑lap bands). If the cylinder wall is worn beyond the first allowable oversize or the finish is inadequate, re‑grinding is required.

faqs.question: What are the standard oversize increments used for aircraft cylinder re‑grinding?
faqs.answer: Typical oversize increments are 0.010 in, 0.015 in, 0.020 in, and 0.030 in. The exact sizes allowed depend on the engine manufacturer’s overhaul manual; some manufacturers may not permit any re‑grind oversize at all.

faqs.question: What is nitriding and why must it not be removed during grinding?
faqs.answer: Nitriding is a surface‑hardening process that hardens the steel surface of the cylinder wall to a depth of several thousandths of an inch. Removing the nitrided layer would reduce wear resistance, so the grinding process must leave this hardened surface intact.

faqs.question: How do I calculate the required re‑grind bore size for a cylinder?
faqs.answer: First obtain the standard bore size from the manufacturer’s specifications. Add the desired oversize to that number. For example, a standard bore of 3.875 in with a 0.015 in oversize requires a re‑grind to 3.890 in (3.875 + 0.015). A tolerance of ±0.0005 in is normally accepted.

faqs.question: What tolerance is acceptable for the final cylinder bore after grinding?
faqs.answer: A tolerance of ±0.0005 in (±0.5 thousandths of an inch) is generally accepted for aircraft cylinder grinding.

faqs.question: How does the amount of wear in the cylinder affect the choice of oversize?
faqs.answer: If any area of the cylinder wall is worn larger than the first oversize, the next larger oversize must be selected so the entire bore can be cleaned up uniformly.

faqs.question: What finish levels are typical for aircraft cylinder walls and how are they measured?
faqs.answer: Most aircraft cylinders are ground to a finish of 15–20 micro‑inch RMS. Low‑powered engines may be 20–30 micro‑inch RMS, while some manufacturers require a super‑finish of 4–6 micro‑inch RMS. The finish is measured in micro‑inch root‑mean‑square (RMS), which represents the average depth of the grinding scratches.

faqs.question: What does “micro‑inch RMS” mean?
faqs.answer: Micro‑inch RMS (root‑mean‑square) quantifies the average depth of surface scratches on the cylinder wall. One micro‑inch RMS corresponds to scratches that are one‑millionth of an inch (0.000001 in) deep.

faqs.question: What is a “choked bore” and why is it used in some cylinder grinding machines?
faqs.answer: A choked bore is a tapered grind where the cylinder’s internal diameter is slightly smaller at the top than at the bottom. This taper compensates for greater thermal expansion at the top during operation, helping to keep the cylinder wall straight as the engine heats up.

faqs.question: How much material should be allowed for honing after a cylinder is ground?
faqs.answer: Typically, 0.001 in of material is removed during honing. For example, if a final bore of 3.890 in is desired, the re‑grind should be specified at 3.889 in, then honed to reach 3.890 in.

summary.title: Aircraft Cylinder Regrinding: Oversizes, Finishes, and Valve Lapping Issues
summary.long_summary: The passage explains how mechanics must identify when an aircraft cylinder requires regrinding and distinguish between acceptable and faulty work. Standard oversize increments for aircraft cylinders are 0.010, 0.015, 0.020, or 0.030 inches, but each manufacturer specifies which are permissible; some prohibit regrinding altogether. The allowable oversize is found in the overhaul manual or parts catalog. To calculate the regrind size, add the chosen oversize to the standard bore (e.g., a 3.875‑in bore with a 0.015‑in oversize becomes 3.890 in), typically with a tolerance of ±0.0005 in. If wear exceeds the first oversize, the next larger oversize must be used. Finish requirements also vary: some engines accept a rougher wall that aids ring seating, while others demand a smooth finish for precise lapping, affecting cost. Cylinder wall finish is measured in micro‑inch RMS; most aircraft are ground to 15–20 µin RMS, low‑power engines may be 20–30 µin RMS, and high‑spec engines may require a superfinish of 4–6 µin RMS. Grinding is performed with a rotating stone whose offset determines the bore size; machines may produce straight or choked (tapered) bores to compensate for thermal expansion. After grinding, honing may be required to achieve the final finish, typically allowing a 0.001 in material removal allowance. The text also includes a figure showing common valve‑lapping defects—fuzzy edge, too narrow contact, and excessive lap bands—along with their causes and remedies.

summary.title: Maximum Allowable Repair Limits for Compressor Blades
summary.long_summary:
The figure presents the maximum permissible repair dimensions for compressor blades, expressed as either radius (R) or depth (D). The limits are organized by blade area (A‑E), blade material (steel or titanium), and machining stage (1‑4 or 5‑9). 

- **Area A**: Steel and titanium blades may be repaired up to 5/16 inch radius in stages 1‑4 and 1/4 inch radius in stages 5‑9. 
- **Area B**: All combinations allow a 1/32 inch depth removal regardless of material or stage. 
- **Area C**: Steel and titanium blades permit 5/32 inch depth in stages 1‑4 and 1/8 inch depth in stages 5‑9. 
- **Area D**: Steel blades allow .008 inch depth (stages 1‑4) and .005 inch depth (stages 5‑9); titanium blades have no allowable removal. 
- **Area E**: Uniformly limited to 1/32 inch depth for both materials and all stages. 

A caution note clarifies that the limits for areas C and E apply only to local, isolated damage and must not be interpreted as permission to remove material across the entire tip or leading/trailing edges in a single cut. The dimensions are controlled by the depth limit, and the table includes references to concave/convex surfaces, fillet areas, and approximate centerlines. Figures 10‑57 and 10‑58 illustrate typical repair limits and example repairs, respectively.

sentiment.summary: Valve overlap variations cause uneven air‑fuel mixtures across cylinders, affecting performance; hydraulic lifters help, and troubleshooting steps are outlined.

faqs.question: How does variation in valve overlap affect the air‑fuel mixture between cylinders?
faqs.answer: Variation in valve overlap changes the amount of time the intake and exhaust valves are open together, which alters the air‑fuel ratio delivered to each cylinder. Cylinders with too little valve clearance (and therefore less overlap) tend to run rich, while those with too much clearance (more overlap) tend to run lean, producing extreme mixture differences across the engine.

faqs.question: Why do cylinders with too little valve clearance run rich?
faqs.answer: When valve clearance is too small, the overlap is reduced, allowing less exhaust gas to escape and less fresh charge to be drawn in during the overlap period. This results in a richer mixture because the carburetor still supplies the same overall mixture to all cylinders.

faqs.question: Why do cylinders with too much valve clearance run lean?
faqs.answer: Excessive valve clearance increases valve overlap, causing more of the fresh charge to be lost out the exhaust during the overlap period. Consequently, less fuel‑air mixture remains in the cylinder, making the mixture lean.

faqs.question: What impact does valve clearance have on volumetric efficiency?
faqs.answer: Variations in valve clearance affect how much air‑fuel enters and how exhaust gases leave each cylinder. Any imbalance reduces the amount of fresh charge that can be drawn in, lowering the cylinder’s volumetric efficiency.

faqs.question: How do hydraulic valve lifters improve engine operation?
faqs.answer: Hydraulic lifters automatically adjust valve clearance, keeping it within a narrow range. This reduces the variation in valve overlap and clearance, leading to more consistent air‑fuel mixtures and better volumetric efficiency. Engines with hydraulic lifters usually require little or no maintenance.

faqs.question: What are the limitations of hydraulic lifters?
faqs.answer: Hydraulic lifters can only control valve clearance within a limited range. If they become stuck in one position, they may fail to maintain proper clearance and become a source of engine trouble.

faqs.question: What is the general approach to engine troubleshooting according to the text?
faqs.answer: Engine troubleshooting is a systematic analysis of symptoms that indicate malfunction. It relies on a thorough knowledge of engine systems and logical reasoning to identify the most common malfunctions, their probable causes, and appropriate corrective actions.

faqs.question: How can manifold pressure and tachometer readings indicate a change in engine power input?
faqs.answer: For a given RPM, any change in power input is reflected by a corresponding change in manifold pressure. The tachometer shows engine speed, while the manifold pressure gauge measures the pressure of the incoming air‑fuel charge; together they provide a measure of engine air consumption and thus power input.

faqs.question: What factors determine propeller load, the measure of engine power output?
faqs.answer: Propeller load depends on propeller RPM, blade angle, and air density. These factors together determine how much power the propeller absorbs from the engine.

faqs.question: Why is it important to consider power settings when diagnosing engine difficulties?
faqs.answer: The power setting at which a difficulty occurs often points to the part of the powerplant that is the root cause. For example, problems that appear only at low power may be related to valve clearance or mixture, while issues at high power might involve airflow or propeller load.

summary.title: Impact of Valve Overlap and Clearance on Air‑Fuel Mixture and Engine Performance
summary.long_summary:
Variations in valve overlap between cylinders produce uneven air‑fuel ratios, especially at idle and low‑power settings, because a single carburetor supplies the same mixture to all cylinders. Cylinders with insufficient clearance run rich, while those with excessive clearance run lean, creating extreme mixture disparities as shown in Figure 10‑51. Valve clearance also influences volumetric efficiency; any inconsistency in intake or exhaust flow reduces the amount of air a cylinder can process. Hydraulic valve lifters mitigate these problems by automatically setting clearance, greatly improving engine operation, though they have a limited adjustment range and can become stuck, potentially causing trouble. Engines equipped with hydraulic lifters generally require little maintenance. 

Engine troubleshooting involves systematic analysis of symptoms to identify common malfunctions. Figure 10‑52 lists typical problems (e.g., failure to start) with probable causes and corrective actions, prioritized by frequency, accessibility, and complexity. Powerplant performance issues often point to the subsystem operating at the problematic power setting. Since cylinders and any supercharging act as an air pump, engine power correlates directly with air consumption. Manifold pressure and tachometer readings provide a proxy for air intake at a given RPM; changes in manifold pressure reflect changes in power input. Propeller load—determined by propeller RPM, blade angle, and air density—measures power output. Monitoring these parameters helps diagnose and correct issues related to valve overlap, clearance, and overall engine efficiency.

With the governor control set for full low pitch, the propeller operates as a fixed-pitch propeller, because the engine is static. Under these conditions, the manifold pressure for any specific engine, with the mixture control in rich, indicates whether all the cylinders are operating properly. With one or more dead or intermittently firing cylinders, the operating cylinders must provide more power for a given rpm. Consequently, the carburetor throttle must be opened further, resulting in higher manifold pressure. Different engines of the same model using the same propeller installation, and at the same barometer and temperature readings, should require the same manifold pressure to within 1 "Hg. A higher than normal manifold pressure usually indicates a dead cylinder or late ignition timing. An excessively low manifold pressure for a particular rpm usually indicates that the ignition timing is early. Early ignition can cause detonation and loss of power at takeoff power settings.

The accuracy of the power check may be affected by the following variables:

1. Wind—any appreciable air movement (5 mph or more) changes the air load on the propeller blade when it is in the fixed-pitch position. A head wind increases the rpm obtainable with a given manifold pressure. A tail wind decreases the rpm.
2. Atmospheric temperatures—the effects of variations in atmospheric temperature tend to cancel each other. Higher carburetor intake and cylinder temperatures tend to lower the rpm, but the propeller load is lightened because of the less dense air.
3. Engine and induction system temperature—if the cylinder and carburetor temperatures are high because of factors other than atmospheric temperature, a low rpm results since the power is lowered without a compensating lowering of the propeller load.
4. Oil temperature—cold oil tends to hold down the rpm, since the higher viscosity results in increased friction horsepower losses.

If the wind is not too strong, the idle mixture setting can be checked easily during the ground check as follows:

1. Close throttle.
2. Move the mixture control to the idle cutoff position and observe the change in rpm. Return the mixture control back to the rich position before engine cutoff.

As the mixture control lever is moved into idle cutoff, and before normal dropoff, one of two things may occur momentarily:

1. The engine speed may increase. An increase in rpm, but less than that recommended by the manufacturer (usually 20 rpm), indicates proper mixture strength. A greater increase indicates that the mixture is too rich.
2. The engine speed may not increase or may drop immediately. This indicates that the idle mixture is too lean. The idle mixture should be set to give a mixture slightly richer than best power, resulting in a 10- to 20-rpm rise after idle cutoff.

### Engine Stopping

With each type of engine installation, specific procedures are used in stopping the engine. The general procedure, outlined in the following paragraphs, reduces the time required for stopping, minimizes backfiring tendencies, and prevents overheating of tightly baffled air-cooled engine during operation on the ground.

In stopping any aircraft engine, the controls are set as follows, irrespective of the type or fuel system installation.

1. Cowl flaps and any other shutters or doors are always placed in the full open position to avoid overheating the engine and are left in that position after the engine is stopped to prevent engine residual heat from deteriorating the ignition system.
2. Carburetor air-heater control is left in the cold position to prevent damage that may occur from backfire.
3. Constant speed propeller is usually stopped with the control set in the high pitch (decrease rpm) position to prevent exposure and corrosion of the pitch changing mechanism.

No mention is made of the throttle, mixture control, fuel selector valve, and ignition switches in the preceding set of directions because the operation of these controls varies with the type of carburetor used with the engine. An engine equipped with a carburetor incorporating an idle cutoff mixture control is stopped as follows:

1. Idle the engine by setting the throttle for 800 to 1,000 rpm.

### Idle Speed & Idle Mixture Checks

Plug fouling difficulty is the inevitable result of failure to provide a proper idle mixture setting. The tendency seems to be to adjust the idle mixture on the extremely rich side and to compensate for this by adjusting the throttle stop to a relatively high rpm for minimum idling. With a properly adjusted idle mixture setting, it is possible to run the engine at idle rpm for long periods. Such a setting results in a minimum of plug fouling and exhaust smoking, and it pays dividends from the savings on the aircraft brakes after landing and while taxiing.
