summary.title: Engine Manifold Pressure Checks, Idle Mixture, and Stopping Procedures
summary.long_summary:
When the governor is set to full low pitch, the propeller behaves as a fixed‑pitch device because the engine is static. Under these conditions, manifold pressure (with the mixture in rich) serves as an indicator of cylinder performance. If one or more cylinders are dead or mis‑firing, the remaining cylinders must work harder, causing the throttle to open further and manifold pressure to rise. Identical engines with the same propeller, barometric pressure, and temperature should show manifold pressures within ±1 in Hg; a higher reading usually signals a dead cylinder or late ignition timing, while an unusually low reading suggests early ignition, which can lead to detonation and power loss.

Factors that can affect the accuracy of a power check include:
1. Wind – headwinds raise rpm for a given manifold pressure, tailwinds lower it.
2. Atmospheric temperature – higher temperatures lower rpm but also reduce air density, partially offsetting the effect.
3. Engine and induction system temperature – excessive cylinder or carburetor heat lowers rpm without reducing propeller load.
4. Oil temperature – cold, viscous oil increases friction and drags rpm down.

If wind is light, the idle mixture can be verified on the ground:
1. Close the throttle.
2. Move the mixture lever to idle‑cutoff and note the rpm change, then return it to rich before shutdown.
A brief rpm increase of less than the manufacturer’s recommended 20 rpm indicates a proper mixture; a larger rise means the mixture is too rich. No increase or an immediate drop shows the mixture is too lean. The idle mixture should be set slightly richer than best‑power, producing a 10‑20 rpm rise after idle‑cutoff.

Engine stopping procedures are standardized to minimize stopping time, prevent back‑firing, and avoid overheating air‑cooled engines. Regardless of engine type, set cowl flaps and any shutters fully open, leave the carburetor air‑heater cold, and, for constant‑speed props, place the prop lever in high‑pitch (low‑rpm) to protect the pitch mechanism. Throttle, mixture, fuel selector, and ignition switch positions vary with carburetor design and are therefore omitted from the generic steps.

For engines with an idle‑cutoff mixture control, stop the engine by idling at 800‑1,000 rpm before shutdown.

Proper idle‑mixture adjustment prevents plug fouling. Over‑rich idle settings lead to excessive throttle stops and increased plug deposits, while a correctly set idle mixture allows the engine to run at low rpm for extended periods with minimal fouling, reduced exhaust smoke, and lower brake wear during taxi and after landing.

As higher powers are approached, a point is reached where the airflow around the cylinders do not provide sufficient cooling. At this point, a secondary cooling method must be used. This secondary cooling is done by enriching the air-fuel mixture beyond the best-power point. Although enriching the mixture to this extent results in a power loss, both power and economy must be sacrificed for engine cooling purposes.

Many older, large, high-powered radial engines were influenced by the cooling requirements on air-fuel mixture, by effects of water injection. Figure 10-46 shows an air-fuel curve for a water-injection engine. The dotted portion of the curve shows how the air-fuel mixture is leaned out during water injection. This leaning is possible because water, rather than extra fuel, is used as a cylinder coolant. These types of systems are not used on modern aircraft.

This permits leaning out to approximately best-power mixture without danger of overheating or detonation. This leaning out gives an increase in power. The water does not alter the combustion characteristics of the mixture. Fuel added to the auto-rich mixture in the power range during dry operation is solely for cooling. A leaner mixture would give more power. Actually, water or, more accurately, the antidetonant (water-alcohol) mixture is a better coolant than extra fuel. Therefore, water injection permits higher manifold pressures and a still further increase in power.

In establishing the final curve for engine operation, the engine's ability to cool itself at various power settings is, of course, taken into account. Sometimes the mixture must be altered for a given installation to compensate for the effect of cowl design, cooling airflow, or other factors on engine cooling. The final air-fuel mixture curves take into account economy, power, engine cooling, idling characteristics, and all other factors that affect combustion.

Figure 10-47. Typical air-fuel mixture curve for a float-type carburetor.

Figure 10-47 shows a typical final curve for a float-type carburetor. Note that the air-fuel mixture at idle is the same in rich and in manual lean. The mixture remains the same until the low cruise range is reached. At this point, the curves separate and then remain parallel through the cruise and power ranges.

Note the spread between the rich and lean setting in the cruise range of both curves. Because of this spread, there is a decrease in power when the mixture control is moved from auto-rich to auto-lean with the engine operating in the cruise range. This is true because the auto-rich setting in the cruise range is very near the best power mixture ratio.

sentiment.summary: The text explains how air‑fuel mixtures affect engine temperature, power, and cooling, including water‑injection effects and typical carburetor mixture curves.

faqs.question: Why is the air‑fuel mixture enriched beyond the best‑power point at high power settings?
faqs.answer: At high power the airflow around the cylinders no longer provides enough cooling, so the mixture is enriched to add extra fuel that acts as a coolant. This secondary cooling is necessary even though it reduces power.

faqs.question: How does water injection affect the air‑fuel mixture and engine cooling?
faqs.answer: Water injection allows the mixture to be leaned out because the water (or water‑alcohol antidetonant) absorbs heat and cools the cylinders. This cooling lets the engine operate near the best‑power mixture without overheating, increasing power.

faqs.question: What is the purpose of leaning the mixture during water injection?
faqs.answer: Leaning is possible because water, not extra fuel, provides the cooling. By leaning the mixture while water is injected, the engine can stay close to the optimal power ratio without the risk of overheating or detonation.

faqs.question: Why were water‑injection systems used on older large radial engines but not on modern aircraft?
faqs.answer: Older high‑powered radial engines relied on water injection to meet cooling requirements at high power. Modern aircraft use different cooling designs and engine technologies, so water‑injection systems are no longer needed.

faqs.question: How is the final air‑fuel mixture curve established for an engine?
faqs.answer: The final curve is drawn after considering the engine’s ability to cool itself at each power setting, as well as factors such as cowl design, cooling airflow, economy, power, idling characteristics, and overall combustion performance.

faqs.question: What does the “auto‑rich” setting represent on the mixture curves?
faqs.answer: “Auto‑rich” is the mixture position near the peak of the power curve; it is the richest mixture that still gives the best power output for a given power range.

faqs.question: How does moving the mixture control from auto‑rich to auto‑lean affect power during cruise?
faqs.answer: In the cruise range, auto‑rich is very close to the best‑power mixture. Shifting to auto‑lean leans the mixture further, which reduces power because the mixture becomes less optimal for producing maximum power.

faqs.question: Why is the idle mixture the same for both the rich and manual‑lean settings on a float‑type carburetor?
faqs.answer: At idle the carburetor delivers the same mixture regardless of whether the control is set to rich or manual‑lean; the mixture only begins to diverge once the low‑cruise range is reached.

faqs.question: How can cowl design and cooling airflow influence the required air‑fuel mixture?
faqs.answer: Changes in cowl shape or cooling airflow affect how well the engine can dissipate heat, so the mixture may need to be altered (leaned or enriched) to compensate for those cooling differences.

faqs.question: Why does enriching the mixture for cooling result in a loss of power?
faqs.answer: Enriching adds extra fuel that primarily absorbs heat rather than contributing to combustion efficiency, so while it cools the engine, it also reduces the overall power output.

summary.title: Air‑Fuel Mixture, Engine Cooling, and Water Injection Effects
summary.long_summary: Figures 10‑45 to 10‑47 illustrate how head temperature and power output vary with air‑fuel mixture and how water injection modifies these relationships. In cruise power, the head temperature rises as the mixture is leaned past the best‑power (auto‑rich) point; insufficient airflow cooling forces the pilot to enrich the mixture beyond best‑power to provide secondary cooling, sacrificing power and fuel economy. Older high‑powered radial engines used water injection (Fig. 10‑46) to cool cylinders without adding fuel. During water injection the mixture can be leaned toward the best‑power setting because the water‑alcohol antidetonant absorbs heat, allowing higher manifold pressures and increased power. The final air‑fuel curves for any engine incorporate cooling capability, cowl design, airflow, economy, idle behavior, and other factors. Figure 10‑47 shows a typical float‑type carburetor curve: idle is very rich, take‑off remains rich, and the mixture leans progressively through cruise. The spread between rich and lean settings in the cruise range means that moving the control from auto‑rich to auto‑lean reduces power, since auto‑rich is close to the optimal power mixture. Overall, engine cooling requirements dictate when mixtures must be enriched or can be leaned, and water injection provides a means to achieve cooler operation while maintaining or increasing power.

sentiment.summary: Table lists engine trouble symptoms, probable causes, and remedies for low power, uneven running, oil pressure, temperature, and consumption issues.

faqs.question: What could cause low power and an uneven running engine?
faqs.answer: Possible causes are a restriction in the exhaust system or improper ignition timing. The remedy is to remove the restriction and check the magnetos for correct timing and synchronization.

faqs.question: Why might an engine fail to develop full power?
faqs.answer: It can be due to a throttle lever out of adjustment, a leak in the induction system, restriction in the carburetor air scoop, improper fuel, a propeller governor out of adjustment, or faulty ignition. Remedies include adjusting the throttle lever, tightening connections, clearing the air scoop, using the recommended fuel, adjusting the governor, and checking ignition timing.

faqs.question: What are common reasons for a rough‑running engine?
faqs.answer: Common reasons are cracked engine mounts, an unbalanced propeller, defective mounting bushings, lead deposits on spark plugs, or an unlocked primer. Fixes involve repairing or replacing mounts, balancing the propeller, installing new bushings, cleaning or replacing plugs, and locking the primer.

faqs.question: How can I diagnose low oil pressure?
faqs.answer: Check for insufficient oil, dirty oil strainers, a defective pressure gauge, air lock or dirt in the relief valve, leaks in suction or pressure lines, high oil temperature, blockage in the oil pump intake, or worn/scored bearings. Remedies include checking oil supply, cleaning strainers, replacing the gauge, cleaning the relief valve, inspecting gaskets, clearing line obstructions, or overhauling the engine.

faqs.question: What actions should be taken for high oil temperature?
faqs.answer: Inspect the air inlet and outlet for deformation or blockage, ensure the oil tank is filled to the proper level, clean oil lines or strainers, examine the sump for metal particles and overhaul the engine if found, replace thermostats, and verify the temperature gauge is functioning.

faqs.question: What might cause excessive oil consumption in an opposed engine?
faqs.answer: Causes include failing or failed bearings, worn or broken piston rings, incorrect installation of piston rings, external oil leaks, leakage through the fuel pump vent, or a faulty engine breather/vacuum pump. Remedies involve checking the sump for metal particles (and overhauling if present), installing new rings, repairing leaking gaskets or O‑rings, replacing the fuel pump seal, and overhauling or replacing the vacuum pump.

faqs.question: How do I know if the oil pressure relief valve needs cleaning?
faqs.answer: If low oil pressure is present and other causes (oil level, strainers, gauge) have been ruled out, the relief valve may be dirty or air‑locked. The remedy is to remove and clean the oil pressure relief valve.

faqs.question: What steps should I follow if the engine’s oil gauge is giving incorrect readings?
faqs.answer: Replace the defective pressure gauge, then re‑check oil pressure after the replacement to confirm proper operation.

faqs.question: Why is it important to lock the primer on a rough‑running engine?
faqs.answer: An unlocked primer can cause rough running; locking the primer is the recommended remedy to eliminate this issue.

faqs.question: What should be done if metal particles are found in the oil sump?
faqs.answer: The presence of metal particles indicates bearing or other internal wear; the engine should be overhauled.

summary.title: Opposed Engine Troubleshooting Guide
summary.long_summary:
The table outlines common problems encountered with opposed engines, their likely causes, and recommended remedies. 

1. **Low power and uneven running** – May result from exhaust restriction or incorrect ignition timing. Remove any blockage in the exhaust and verify magneto timing and synchronization. 

2. **Failure to develop full power** – Possible causes include mis‑adjusted throttle lever, induction leaks, clogged carburetor air scoop, unsuitable fuel, mis‑adjusted propeller governor, or faulty ignition. Adjust the throttle, tighten connections, clear the air scoop, use the specified fuel, set the governor correctly, and check ignition timing. 

3. **Rough running** – Often due to cracked engine mounts, unbalanced propeller, worn mounting bushings, lead deposits on spark plugs, or an unlocked primer. Repair or replace mounts, balance the propeller, install new bushings, clean or replace plugs, and lock the primer. 

4. **Low oil pressure** – Can be caused by low oil level, dirty strainers, a bad pressure gauge, air lock or debris in the relief valve, leaks in suction or pressure lines, high oil temperature, blocked pump intake, or worn bearings. Ensure adequate oil, clean strainers, replace the gauge, clean the relief valve, inspect gaskets, address high temperature issues, clear pump passages, or overhaul the engine if bearings are damaged. 

5. **High oil temperature** – May stem from inadequate air cooling, insufficient oil, clogged lines or strainers, failing bearings, faulty thermostats or temperature gauge, or excessive blow‑by. Verify inlet/outlet airflow, top up oil, clean lines/strainers, inspect the sump for metal particles and overhaul if needed, replace thermostats, and address weak or stuck piston rings. 

6. **Excessive oil consumption** – Typically due to failing bearings, worn or incorrectly installed piston rings, external leaks, fuel pump vent leaks, or breather system problems. Check the sump for metal debris and consider an engine overhaul, install new rings, repair leaking gaskets or O‑rings, replace the fuel pump seal, and service or replace the breather/vacuum pump. 

Overall, the guide provides a systematic approach: identify the symptom, examine the listed probable causes, and apply the corresponding corrective actions to restore engine performance.

sentiment.summary: The passage describes cylinder bore grinding, honing, deglazing, reassembly steps, and testing procedures for aircraft reciprocating engines.

faqs.question: What is cylinder bore grinding and how is it performed?
faqs.answer: Cylinder bore grinding removes material from the cylinder wall by using a rotating stone that moves back‑and‑forth (shown in the left diagram) while also moving in a spiral pattern inside the bore (right diagram).

faqs.question: When should a micromatic hone be used on cylinder walls?
faqs.answer: A micromatic hone can be used to straighten out cylinder walls after grinding because its stones are spring‑loaded and follow the contour of the wall.

faqs.question: Why should a burnishing hone not be used to straighten cylinder walls?
faqs.answer: A burnishing hone should not be used for straightening because, unlike the micromatic hone, it can aggravate a tapered condition rather than correct it.

faqs.question: How is a cross‑hatch pattern created on the cylinder wall and why is it needed?
faqs.answer: A deglazing hone, turned by a drill and moved rapidly in and out of the cylinder, creates a cross‑hatch pattern on the wall. This pattern is required to allow proper piston‑ring break‑in.

faqs.question: What inspections are required after cylinders have been reground or deglazed?
faqs.answer: After regrounding or deglazing, the cylinder size, wall finish, and any signs of overheating or grinding cracks must be checked before the cylinder is installed on an engine.

faqs.question: What is the recommended method for organizing components before engine reassembly?
faqs.answer: All serviceable and new components should be cleaned, organized, and laid out in the exact order of assembly, often at a single workstation with the same technicians completing the whole engine.

faqs.question: Which reference documents should be consulted during engine reassembly?
faqs.answer: The parts catalog should be used to verify correct hardware, and the engine overhaul manual should be consulted for safety‑wire usage, self‑locking nuts, torque values, and lubrication procedures.

faqs.question: What lubrication steps are required during reassembly?
faqs.answer: Components must be pre‑lubricated according to the specifications set forth in the overhaul manual before they are installed.

faqs.question: How is an engine tested to confirm it is ready for airworthy service?
faqs.answer: Testing typically requires a test stand or test cell, although the aircraft itself can be used, to verify that the engine is in excellent mechanical condition before returning to service.

faqs.question: Can the aircraft be used as a test stand for engine testing?
faqs.answer: Yes, while a dedicated test stand or test cell is the usual method, the aircraft can also be employed to perform the necessary engine‑readiness tests.

summary.title: Cylinder Bore Preparation, Engine Reassembly, and Testing Procedures
summary.long_summary:
The passage outlines the processes involved in preparing cylinder bores and reassembling an engine. Figure 10‑30 illustrates cylinder bore grinding, where a rotating stone moves back‑and‑forth in a cross‑section view and follows a spiral path in a top‑down view to remove material. Micromatic hones can straighten cylinder walls, but burnishing hones should not be used for this purpose because spring‑loaded stones may follow the wall contour and worsen tapering. Deglazing hones create a cross‑hatch pattern on the cylinder wall to aid piston‑ring break‑in; this is done by rapidly moving a drill‑driven hone in and out of the cylinder (Figure 10‑32). After grinding or deglazing, the cylinder size, wall finish, and any signs of overheating or cracks must be inspected before engine installation.

Reassembly requires cleaning, organizing, and laying out all serviceable and new components in assembly order. A common practice is to assemble the engine at a single workstation with the same technicians handling the entire build. The parts catalog must be consulted to ensure correct hardware, and the overhaul manual provides guidance on safety wire, self‑locking nuts, torque values, and pre‑lubrication. All manufacturer‑specified procedures and checks must be followed.

Figure 10‑31 shows cylinder honing, where a rotating stone moves back‑and‑forth and spirally to produce the required cross‑hatch pattern. Finally, the installation and testing phase involves verifying that the engine is ready for airworthy service. This typically requires a test stand or test cell, though the aircraft itself can be used for testing. The overall goal is to ensure the engine is mechanically sound and meets all performance standards before return to service.

All measurements involving cylinder barrel diameters must be taken at a minimum of two positions 90° apart in the particular plane being measured. It may be necessary to take more than two measurements to determine the maximum wear.

Taper of the cylinder walls is the difference between the diameter of the cylinder barrel at the bottom and the diameter at the top. The cylinder is usually worn larger at the top than at the bottom. This taper is caused by the natural wear pattern. At the top of the stroke, the piston is subjected to greater heat and pressure and more erosive environment than at the bottom of the stroke. Also, there is greater freedom of movement at the top of the stroke. Under these conditions, the piston wears the cylinder wall more at the top of the cylinder. In most cases, the taper ends with a ridge, that must be removed during overhaul. [Figure 10-6]

Where cylinders are built with an intentional choke, measurement of taper becomes more complicated. Cylinder choke is where the top of the cylinder has been made with the very top diameter of the cylinder smaller, to compensate for wear and expansion during operation. It is necessary to know exactly how the size indicates wear or taper. Taper can be measured in any cylinder by a cylinder dial gauge as long as there is not a sharp step. The dial gauge tends to ride up on the step and causes inaccurate readings at the top of the cylinder.

The measurement for out-of-roundness is usually taken at the top of the cylinder. However, a reading should also be taken at the skirt of the cylinder to detect dents or bends caused by careless handling. A step, or ridge, is formed in the cylinder by the wearing action of the piston rings. [Figure 10-6] The greatest wear is at the top of the ring travel limit. The ridge that results is likely to cause damage to the rings or piston. If the step exceeds tolerances, it should be removed by grinding the cylinder oversize, or it should be blended by hand-stoning to break the sharp edge.

A step also may be found where the bottom ring reaches the lowest travel. This step is rarely found to be excessive, but it should be checked.

Inspect the cylinder walls for rust, pitting, or scores. Mild damage of this sort can be removed when the cylinders are deglazed. With more extensive damage, the cylinder has to be reground or honed. If the damage is too deep to be removed by either of these methods, the cylinder usually will have to be rejected. Most engine manufacturers, or engine overhaul repair stations, have an exchange service on cylinders with damaged barrels.

Check the cylinder flange for warpage by placing the cylinder on a suitable jig. Check to see that the flange contacts the jig all the way around. The amount of warpage can be checked by using a thickness gauge. A cylinder whose flange is warped beyond the limits should be rejected.

Rocker Arms & Shafts

Inspect the valve rockers for cracks and worn, pitted, or scored tips. See that all oil passages are free from obstructions.

Inspect the shaft's diameter for correct size with a micrometer. Rocker shafts are often found to be scored and burned because of excessive turning in the cylinder head. Also, there may be some pickup on the shaft (bronze from the rocker bushing transferred to the steel shaft). Generally, this is caused by overheating and too little clearance between shaft and bushing. The clearance between the shaft and the bushing is most important.

Inspect the rocker arm bushing for correct size. Check for proper clearance between the shaft and the bushing. Very often the bushings are scored because of mishandling during disassembly. Check to see that the oil holes line up. At least 50% of the hole in the bushing should align with the hole in the rocker arm.

On engines that use a bearing, rather than a bushing, inspect the bearing to make certain it has not been turning in the rocker arm boss. Also inspect the bearing to determine its serviceability.

faqs.question: How many positions must be used when measuring cylinder barrel diameters?
faqs.answer: Measurements must be taken at a minimum of two positions 90° apart in the plane being measured, and additional positions may be needed to determine the maximum wear.

faqs.question: Why is the cylinder usually larger at the top than at the bottom?
faqs.answer: The top of the cylinder experiences higher heat, pressure, and a more erosive environment, plus greater freedom of movement, causing the piston to wear the cylinder wall more at the top.

faqs.question: What is cylinder taper and how is it measured?
faqs.answer: Taper is the difference between the bottom and top diameters of the cylinder barrel. It can be measured with a cylinder dial gauge as long as there is no sharp step that would cause the gauge to ride up and give inaccurate readings.

faqs.question: How does an intentional choke affect taper measurement?
faqs.answer: When a cylinder is built with an intentional choke (the top diameter is made smaller), measuring taper becomes more complicated because the size must be interpreted to distinguish wear from the built‑in taper.

faqs.question: Where should out‑of‑roundness be measured on a cylinder?
faqs.answer: Out‑of‑roundness is usually measured at the top of the cylinder, and a reading should also be taken at the skirt to detect dents or bends caused by handling.

faqs.question: What action should be taken if a step or ridge exceeds tolerance?
faqs.answer: If the step exceeds tolerances, it should be removed by grinding the cylinder oversize or by hand‑stoning to blend and break the sharp edge.

faqs.question: How are minor and severe cylinder‑wall damages handled?
faqs.answer: Mild rust, pitting, or scores can be removed during deglazing. More extensive damage requires regrounding or honing, and damage too deep for those methods usually leads to cylinder rejection, with many manufacturers offering an exchange service.

faqs.question: How can cylinder flange warpage be checked?
faqs.answer: Place the cylinder on a suitable jig and verify that the flange contacts the jig all the way around; use a thickness gauge to measure any deviation. A flange warped beyond the specified limits must be rejected.

faqs.question: What should be inspected on valve rocker arms during overhaul?
faqs.answer: Inspect the rocker arms for cracks and for worn, pitted, or scored tips, and ensure all oil passages are free of obstructions.

faqs.question: Why is clearance between the rocker shaft and its bushing important, and how is it verified?
faqs.answer: Clearance is critical because insufficient clearance can cause overheating, scoring, and pickup of bronze from the bushing onto the steel shaft. Verify the shaft diameter with a micrometer, check the bushing size, and ensure proper clearance; also confirm that at least 50 % of the oil hole in the bushing aligns with the hole in the rocker arm.

summary.title: Cylinder Bore Inspection and Rocker Arm Guidelines
summary.long_summary:
The passage describes proper procedures for inspecting and measuring engine cylinder bores and related rocker arm components. A cylinder bore gauge is used to record bore diameter, step, and fit between piston skirt and cylinder. Measurements of barrel diameters must be taken at least at two points 90° apart in the same plane, with additional points taken if needed to locate maximum wear. Taper, defined as the difference between top and bottom diameters, typically shows larger wear at the top due to higher heat, pressure, and piston movement. Excessive taper creates a ridge that must be removed during overhaul. When cylinders are intentionally choked (top diameter made smaller to allow for wear), taper measurement becomes more complex; a dial gauge can be used only if no sharp step is present, as the gauge can ride over steps and give false readings. 

Out‑of‑roundness is usually measured at the cylinder top, but readings at the skirt are also required to detect dents or bends. Steps or ridges form where piston rings wear the wall, especially at the top of the ring travel limit; if these exceed tolerances, they must be ground oversize or hand‑stoned to eliminate sharp edges. A lesser step may appear at the bottom ring limit and should be checked. Cylinder walls should be inspected for rust, pitting, or scoring. Minor damage can be removed by de‑glazing; more severe damage requires regrounding or honing, and deep damage may necessitate cylinder rejection or exchange. 

The cylinder flange must be checked for warpage by seating it on a jig and confirming full contact; thickness gauges can quantify warpage, and excessive warpage leads to rejection. 

The document also outlines rocker arm and shaft inspection: valve rockers are examined for cracks, wear, pits, or scores, and oil passages must be clear. Shaft diameters are verified with a micrometer; common issues include scoring, burning, and bronze pickup from rocker bushings due to overheating or insufficient clearance. Correct clearance between shaft and bushing is critical. Rocker arm bushings are checked for proper size, clearance, and oil‑hole alignment (at least 50% overlap). For engines using bearings instead of bushings, bearings are inspected for turning in the rocker arm boss and overall serviceability. Overall, the guidelines ensure accurate measurement of cylinder wear, proper detection of defects, and thorough inspection of rocker components to maintain engine reliability.

Since the thermocouple is attached to only one cylinder, it can do no more than give evidence of general engine temperature. While normally it can be assumed that the remaining cylinder temperatures are lower, conditions such as detonation are not indicated unless they occur in the cylinder that has the thermocouple attached. The cylinder head temperature gauge is a dual gauge that incorporates two separate temperature scales. [Figure 10-39] The scales are calibrated in increments of 10°, with numerals at the 0°, 100°, 200°, and 300° graduations. The space between any two graduation marks represents 10 °C. The blue arc on the gauge indicates the range within which operation is permitted in auto-lean. The bottom of this arc, 100 °C, indicates the minimum desired temperature to ensure efficient engine operation during flight. The top of the blue arc, 230 °C, indicates the temperature at which the mixture control must be moved to the “auto-rich” position. The green arc describes the range within which operation must be in auto-rich. The top of this arc, 248 °C, indicates maximum continuous power; all operation above this temperature is limited in time (usually 5 to 15 minutes). The red line indicates maximum permissible temperature, 260 °C. **Torquemeter** Most torque systems use an oil pressure output from a torque valve to indicate actual engine power output at various power settings. The torquemeter indicates the amount of torque being produced at the propeller shaft. A helical gear moves back and forth as the torque on the propeller shaft varies. This gear, acting on a piston, positions a valve that meters the oil pressure proportionally to the torque being produced. A change in pressure from the valve that is connected to a transducer is then converted to an electrical signal and is transmitted to the flight deck. The torquemeter can read out in foot-pounds of torque, percent of horsepower, or horsepower. The earlier systems read out in psi, and the flight engineer converted this to the correct power setting. [Figure 10-40] Some systems use strain gauges to attach to the ring gear to provide an electrical signal directly to the readout. **Warning Systems** Many of the miscellaneous gauges and devices indicate only that a system is functioning or has failed to function. On some aircraft, a warning light illuminates when the fuel pressure or oil pressure is low. **Reciprocating Engine Operation** The operation of the powerplant is controlled from the flight deck. Some installations have numerous control handles and levers connected to the engine by rods, cables, bellcranks, pulleys, etc. In most cases, the control handles are conveniently mounted on quadrants in the flight deck. Placards, or markings, are placed on the quadrant to indicate the functions and positions of the levers. In some installations, friction clutches are installed to hold the controls in place. **Engine Instruments** The term engine instruments usually includes all instruments required to measure and indicate the functioning of the powerplant. The engine instruments are generally installed on the instrument panel so that all of them can easily be observed at one time. Manifold pressure, rpm, engine temperature, oil temperature, CAT, and the air-fuel ratio can be controlled by manipulating the flight deck controls. Coordinating the movement of the controls with the instrument readings protects against exceeding operating limits. Engine operation is usually limited by specified operating ranges of the following: 1. Crankshaft speed (rpm). 2. Manifold pressure.

faqs.question: How does a torquemeter determine the torque being produced at the propeller shaft?
faqs.answer: A helical gear moves back and forth with shaft torque, acting on a piston that positions a valve. The valve meters oil pressure proportionally to the torque; this pressure is converted by a transducer into an electrical signal that is displayed on the flight deck.

summary.title: Engine Temperature Gauge, Torquemeter, and Control Systems Overview
summary.long_summary:
The cylinder head temperature (CHT) gauge is a dual‑scale instrument calibrated in 10 °C increments, with numeric marks at 0, 100, 200 and 300 °C. Colored arcs define operating zones: a blue arc (100‑230 °C) indicates the permissible range for auto‑lean operation, a green arc (230‑248 °C) marks the auto‑rich range, and a red line at 260 °C shows the maximum allowable temperature. The thermocouple attached to a single cylinder can only provide a general engine temperature indication; it cannot detect detonation in other cylinders.

The torquemeter measures propeller‑shaft torque by converting oil‑pressure variations, generated by a helical gear acting on a piston, into an electrical signal. Readouts may be in foot‑pounds, percent horsepower, or horsepower; some older systems displayed pressure in psi, which the flight engineer translated to power. Strain‑gauge versions attach directly to the ring gear.

Various warning lights alert the crew to low fuel or oil pressure. Reciprocating‑engine controls are typically mounted on flight‑deck quadrants with placards indicating lever functions; friction clutches may hold positions. Engine instruments—including manifold pressure, RPM, CHT, oil temperature, CAT, and air‑fuel ratio—are grouped on the instrument panel for simultaneous monitoring, ensuring operation stays within limits for crankshaft speed and manifold pressure.

the idle cutoff or full lean position. When the engine ceases firing, turn off both ignition and master switches. Record the cylinder head temperature reading registered on the flight deck gauge. As soon as the propeller has ceased rotating, apply the instrument to each cylinder head, and record the relative temperature of each cylinder. Start with number one and proceed in numerical order around the engine, as rapidly as possible. To obtain comparative temperature values, a firm contact must be made at the same relative location on each cylinder. Note any outstandingly low (cold) values. Compare the temperature readings to determine which cylinders are dead (cold cylinders) or are operating intermittently.

Difficulties that may cause a cylinder to be inoperative (dead) when isolated to one magneto, either the right or left positions, are:

  1. Defective spark plugs.
  2. Incorrect valve clearances.
  3. Leaking intake pipes.
  4. Lack of compression.
  5. Defective spark plug lead.
  6. Defective fuel-injection nozzle.

Repeat the cold cylinder test for the other magneto positions on the ignition switch, if necessary. Cooling the engine between tests is unnecessary. The airflow created by the propeller, and the cooling effect of the incoming air-fuel mixture is sufficient to cool any cylinders that are functioning on one test and not functioning on the next.

In interpreting the results of a cold cylinder check, remember that the temperatures are relative. A cylinder temperature taken alone means little, but when compared with the temperatures of other cylinders on the same engine, it provides valuable diagnostic information. The readings shown in Figure 10-56 illustrate this point. On this check, the cylinder head temperature gauge reading at the time the engine was shut down was 160 °C on both tests.

A review of these temperature readings reveals that, on the right magneto, cylinder number 3 runs cool and cylinders 5 and 6 run cold. This indicates that cylinder 3 is firing intermittently, and cylinders 5 and 6 are dead during engine operation on the plugs fired by the right magneto. Cylinders 4 and 6 are dead during operation on the plugs fired by the left magneto. Cylinder 6 is completely dead. An ignition system operational check would not disclose this dead cylinder, since the cylinder is inoperative on both right and left switch positions.

A dead cylinder can be detected during run-up, since an engine with a dead cylinder requires a higher than normal manifold pressure to produce any given rpm below the cut-in speed of the propeller governor. A dead cylinder could also be detected by comparing power input and power output with the aid of a torquemeter.

Defects within the ignition system that can cause a cylinder to go completely dead are:

  1. Both spark plugs inoperative.
  2. Both ignition leads grounded, leaking, or open.
  3. A combination of inoperative spark plugs and defective ignition leads.
  4. Faulty fuel-injection nozzles, incorrect valve clearances, and other defects outside the ignition system.

In interpreting the readings obtained on a cold cylinder check, the amount the engine cools during the check must be considered. To determine the extent to which this factor should be considered in evaluating the readings, re-check some of the first cylinders tested, and compare the final readings with those made at the start of the check. Another factor to be considered is the normal variation in temperature between cylinders and between rows. This variation results from those design features that affect the airflow past the cylinders.

Turbine Engine Maintenance

Turbine powerplant maintenance procedures vary widely according to the design and construction of the particular engine being serviced. The detailed procedures recommended by the engine manufacturer should be followed when performing inspections or maintenance. Maintenance information presented in this section is not intended to specify the exact manner in which maintenance operations are to be performed but is included to convey a general idea of the procedures involved. For inspection purposes, the turbine engine is divided into two main sections: the cold and hot.

faqs.question: What is the purpose of a cold cylinder check?

faqs.question: How are the temperature readings taken during a cold cylinder check?

faqs.question: Why is it important to compare temperatures rather than look at a single cylinder’s reading?
faqs.answer: Temperatures are relative; a single reading tells little, but when compared with the other cylinders it reveals which cylinders are cooler (indicating intermittent firing) or cold (indicating they are dead).

faqs.question: Based on Figure 10‑56, which cylinders are dead or intermittent on the right magneto?
faqs.answer: On the right magneto, cylinder 3 runs cool (intermittent), and cylinders 5 and 6 run cold (dead).

faqs.question: Which cylinders are dead on the left magneto according to the same data?

faqs.question: What are common causes of a cylinder being dead when only one magneto is selected?
faqs.answer: Possible causes include defective spark plugs, incorrect valve clearances, leaking intake pipes, lack of compression, defective spark‑plug leads, or a defective fuel‑injection nozzle.

faqs.question: What defects can make a cylinder completely dead on both magnetos?
faqs.answer: A cylinder can be completely dead if both spark plugs are inoperative, both ignition leads are grounded, leaking, or open, a combination of bad plugs and leads, or if there are faulty fuel‑injection nozzles, incorrect valve clearances, or other non‑ignition‑system defects.

faqs.question: Do I need to let the engine cool between right‑ and left‑magneto cold cylinder tests?
faqs.answer: No. The airflow from the propeller and the cooling effect of the incoming air‑fuel mixture are sufficient to cool any cylinders that were functioning on the first test.

faqs.question: How can a dead cylinder be detected during engine run‑up?
faqs.answer: A dead cylinder causes the engine to require higher than normal manifold pressure to achieve a given RPM below the propeller governor’s cut‑in speed, and it can also be identified by comparing power input and output with a torquemeter.

faqs.question: What should be considered when interpreting the temperature readings from a cold cylinder check?
faqs.answer: Consider the amount of cooling that occurs during the test, normal temperature variation between cylinders and rows due to design‑related airflow differences, and re‑check early cylinders to see if their temperatures have changed.

summary.title: Cold Cylinder Check: Procedure, Results, and Diagnosis
summary.long_summary:
The passage describes how to perform a cold cylinder check on a piston engine and how to interpret the results. After shutting the engine down at idle cutoff or full lean, the pilot records the overall cylinder‑head temperature on the flight‑deck gauge, then quickly touches an instrument to each cylinder head in numerical order, noting the relative temperature at the same spot on each cylinder. The table (Figure 10‑56) shows temperature readings for right and left magneto positions. On the right magneto, cylinder 3 runs cool (intermittent firing) while cylinders 5 and 6 are cold (dead). On the left magneto, cylinders 4 and 6 are dead, confirming cylinder 6 is completely inoperative. The test does not require cooling between magneto positions because propeller airflow and the incoming mixture provide sufficient cooling.

Low or cold readings indicate possible causes such as defective spark plugs, incorrect valve clearances, leaking intake pipes, lack of compression, faulty spark‑plug leads, or bad fuel‑injection nozzles. A completely dead cylinder may result from both plugs failing, both leads being open or grounded, or a combination of plug and lead failures, as well as non‑ignition defects like bad nozzles or valve issues.

Interpretation must consider engine cooling during the test and normal temperature variation between cylinders and rows. Re‑checking early cylinders can help gauge cooling effects. The passage also notes that a dead cylinder raises required manifold pressure during run‑up and can be detected with a torquemeter. Finally, a brief note introduces turbine‑engine maintenance, emphasizing that procedures vary by design and should follow manufacturer guidelines, dividing the engine into cold and hot sections for inspection.

EGT Circuit Error

This error is found by using the EGT and comparing the reading of the aircraft EGT indicator with the analyzer temperature reading. [Figure 10-78] The analyzer and aircraft temperature readings are then compared.

Resistance of Circuit Out of Tolerance

The engine thermocouple circuit resistance is a very important adjustment since a high-resistance condition gives a low indication on the aircraft EGT indicator. Shorts to Ground/Shorts Between Leads

These errors are found by doing the insulation check using an ohmmeter. Resistance values from zero to 550,000 ohms can be read on the insulation check ohmmeter by selecting the proper range.

summary.title: Engine Diagnostic Errors and Tachometer Troubleshooting
summary.long_summary: The passage outlines common engine diagnostic problems and their detection methods. An EGT circuit error is identified by comparing the aircraft’s EGT indicator reading with the analyzer’s temperature reading; discrepancies indicate a fault. Circuit resistance is critical—excessive resistance causes the EGT indicator to read low, masking an over‑temperature condition, so it must be measured and corrected. Shorts to ground or between leads are detected with an insulation‑check ohmmeter, which can read resistances from 0 to 550 kΩ. For tachometer system troubleshooting, the analyzer’s RPM‑check circuit is connected in parallel with the aircraft tachometer leads. During engine run‑up, both the analyzer and the aircraft tachometer display engine speed; readings must agree within the tolerance specified in the technical instructions. If the difference exceeds the allowed tolerance, the engine must be stopped and the fault investigated. The section also references a magnetic pickup and gear assembly used in these diagnostics.

Check the travel of the valve face across the stone. The valve should completely pass the stone on both sides, yet not travel far enough to grind the stem. There are stops on the machine that can be set to control this travel.

With the valve set correctly in place, turn on the machine and the grinding fluid so that it splashes on the valve face. Back the grinding wheel off all the way. Place the valve directly in front of the stone. [Figure 10-25] Slowly bring the wheel forward until a light cut is made on the valve. The intensity of the grind is measured by sound more than anything else. Slowly draw the valve back and forth across the stone without increasing the cut. Move the work head table back and forth using the full face of the stone, but always keep the valve face on the stone. When the sound of the grind diminishes, indicating that some valve material has been removed, move the workhead table to the extreme left to stop rotation of the valve. Inspect the valve to determine if further grinding is necessary. If another cut must be made, bring the valve in front of the stone, then advance the stone out to the valve. Do not increase the cut without having the valve directly in front of the stone.

An important precaution in valve grinding, as in any kind of grinding, is to make light cuts only. Heavy cuts cause chattering, that may make the valve surface so rough that much time is lost in obtaining the desired finish.

After grinding, check the valve margin to be sure that the valve edge has not been ground too thin. A thin edge is called a feather edge and can lead to pre-ignition; the valve edge would burn away in a short period of time, and the cylinder would have to be overhauled again. Figure 10-26 shows a valve with a normal margin and one with a feather edge.

The valve tip may be resurfaced on the valve grinder. The tip is ground to remove cupping or wear, and also to adjust valve clearances on some engines.

faqs.question: How do I set the travel of the valve face across the grinding stone?
faqs.answer: Check that the valve face completely passes the stone on both sides without grinding the stem. Use the machine’s stops to limit the travel range so the valve does not go far enough to contact the stem.

faqs.question: What is the correct way to make the first cut on the valve?
faqs.answer: Turn on the machine and grinding fluid, back the grinding wheel all the way, place the valve directly in front of the stone, then slowly bring the wheel forward until a light cut is made. The cut’s intensity is judged mainly by the sound of the grind.

faqs.question: How can I tell when enough material has been removed from the valve?
faqs.answer: When the grinding sound diminishes, it indicates that some valve material has been removed. At that point, move the work‑head table to the extreme left to stop the valve’s rotation and inspect the valve.

faqs.question: Why should I only make light cuts during valve grinding?
faqs.answer: Heavy cuts cause chattering, which makes the valve surface rough and wastes time trying to achieve the desired finish. Light cuts keep the surface smooth and the process efficient.

faqs.question: What is a ‘feather edge’ and why must it be avoided?
faqs.answer: A feather edge is a valve edge that has been ground too thin. It can lead to pre‑ignition because the thin edge burns away quickly, requiring the cylinder to be overhauled again.

faqs.question: How do I check the valve margin after grinding?
faqs.answer: Inspect the valve edge to ensure it is not overly thin. A normal margin appears thick and flat, while a feather edge looks thin and rounded.

faqs.question: Can the valve tip be ground, and if so, why?
faqs.answer: Yes. The valve tip may be resurfaced on the grinder to remove cupping or wear and to adjust valve clearances on some engines.

faqs.question: What role does grinding fluid play in the grinding process?
faqs.answer: Grinding fluid splashes on the valve face, cooling the material and helping to achieve a smoother cut.

faqs.question: What should I do if another cut is needed after the first inspection?
faqs.answer: Place the valve back in front of the stone, then advance the stone out to the valve and make another light cut. Do not increase the cut depth unless the valve is directly in front of the stone.

faqs.question: How do I prevent the valve stem from being ground?
faqs.answer: Set the machine’s travel stops so the valve face passes the stone fully but does not travel far enough to contact the stem. The ‘In’ stop specifically prevents grinding the stem.

summary.title: Engine Valve Grinding Procedure and Precautions
summary.long_summary: The valve is mounted on the grinding machine’s work‑head table and its travel is adjusted so the valve face passes completely over the stone without reaching the stem, using machine stops. With the valve correctly positioned, the machine and grinding fluid are turned on. The wheel is retracted, the valve placed directly in front of the stone, and the wheel advanced slowly until a light cut is made. The grinding intensity is judged by sound. The valve is then drawn back and forth across the stone, keeping the valve face on the stone and using the full stone face, without increasing the cut depth. When the grinding sound diminishes, indicating material removal, the work‑head is moved to stop valve rotation and the valve is inspected. If further material must be removed, the valve is repositioned and another light cut is made; cuts are never increased without the valve directly in front of the stone. Light cuts are essential; heavy cuts cause chattering and a rough surface, wasting time. After grinding, the valve margin is checked to ensure it is not too thin; a "feather edge" can cause pre‑ignition and premature valve failure. The valve tip may also be resurfaced to remove cupping, wear, or to adjust clearances. Figures illustrate the valve installation, the grinding setup, and the difference between a normal margin and a feather edge.

In the middle row, the left instrument shows percent RPM on a 0‑100 % scale and includes a small sub‑dial for finer reading. The middle‑right gauge measures oil pressure, also on a 0‑100 psi scale. The bottom‑left display is labeled "External Gas Temperature" (EXT GAS TEMP) with a scale from 0 to 10, marked at 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, and 9. Finally, the bottom‑right instrument indicates temperature, spanning –50 °C to 150 °C. Together, these gauges provide a comprehensive visual overview of key engine parameters.

sentiment.summary: Table lists turbojet engine malfunctions, probable causes, and suggested actions for various abnormal parameter readings.

faqs.question: What could cause low rpm, low exhaust gas temperature, and low fuel flow when the engine pressure ratio is set to the expected value?
faqs.answer: The engine pressure ratio indication may have a high reading error. Check the inlet pressure line from the probe to the transmitter for leaks and verify the accuracy of the engine pressure ratio transmitter and indicator.

faqs.question: Why would an engine show high rpm, high exhaust gas temperature, and high fuel flow at the expected engine pressure ratio?
faqs.answer: The engine pressure ratio indication may have a low reading error caused by a misaligned or cracked turbine discharge probe, a leak in the turbine discharge pressure line, an inaccurate transmitter or indicator, or carbon particles in the pressure line or restrictor orifices. Inspect the probe, pressure‑test the line for leaks, and check the transmitter and indicator for accuracy.

faqs.question: What does it indicate if the engine has high exhaust gas temperature, low rpm, and high fuel flow at all engine pressure ratio settings?
faqs.answer: It may indicate turbine damage or loss of turbine efficiency. Confirm by checking the engine coast‑down for abnormal noise and reduced time, and visually inspect the turbine area with a strong light.

faqs.question: If only the exhaust gas temperature is high while other parameters are normal, what is the likely problem?
faqs.answer: The issue may be with the thermocouple leads or the temperature instrument. Re‑calibrate the exhaust gas temperature instrumentation.

faqs.question: What should be done when the engine vibrates throughout the rpm range but the amplitude decreases as rpm is reduced?
faqs.answer: Turbine damage is the probable cause. Inspect the turbine as described for turbine‑damage symptoms.

faqs.question: What is the probable cause of vibration at high rpm and fuel flow when the engine pressure ratio is held constant?
faqs.answer: Damage in the compressor section is likely. Check the compressor section for damage.

faqs.question: What could cause engine vibration that is more pronounced at cruise or idle rpm ranges?
faqs.answer: An engine‑mounted accessory such as a constant‑speed drive, generator, hydraulic pump, etc., may be the source. Check each accessory component in turn.

faqs.question: Why might oil temperature be high even though power‑setting parameters have not changed?
faqs.answer: High oil temperature can be caused by problems with the engine main bearings. Check the scavenge oil filters and magnetic plugs.

faqs.question: What are the possible reasons for higher than normal exhaust gas temperature during takeoff, climb, and cruise, accompanied by higher rpm and fuel flow?
faqs.answer: Possible causes are a malfunctioning engine bleed‑air valve or a leak in the turbine discharge pressure probe or its line to the transmitter. Check the operation of the bleed valve and inspect the probe and pressure line.

faqs.question: What should be done if the engine has high exhaust gas temperature at the target engine pressure ratio for takeoff?
faqs.answer: The engine may be out of trim. Use a jet‑calibration system (jetcal) to check the engine and re‑trim it as desired.

summary.title: Turbojet Engine Troubleshooting Guide
summary.long_summary: The table outlines common turbojet engine malfunctions, their probable causes, and recommended corrective actions. Low rpm, low exhaust gas temperature (EGT), and low fuel flow at the expected engine pressure ratio (EPR) suggest a high‑reading error in the EPR; inspect the inlet pressure line for leaks and verify the transmitter and indicator accuracy. Conversely, high rpm, high EPR, high EGT, and high fuel flow indicate a low‑reading error, often due to a misaligned or cracked turbine discharge probe, leaks in the discharge pressure line, inaccurate transmitter/indicator, or carbon buildup; check probe condition, pressure‑test the line, and verify instrument accuracy. High EGT with low rpm and high fuel flow across all EPR settings points to possible turbine damage or loss of efficiency; confirm by coast‑down noise, reduced coast‑down time, and visual inspection of the turbine. Isolated high EGT may be due to faulty thermocouple leads or instrumentation; recalibrate the EGT sensor. Vibration throughout the rpm range that diminishes with lower rpm also indicates turbine damage; inspect the turbine. Vibration at high rpm and fuel flow with constant EPR suggests compressor damage; examine the compressor section. Vibration that is more pronounced at cruise or idle rpm often originates from engine‑mounted accessories such as constant‑speed drives, generators, or hydraulic pumps; test each component. Unchanged power settings with high oil temperature point to main bearing issues; check scavenge oil filters and magnetic plugs. Elevated EGT during takeoff, climb, or cruise with higher rpm and fuel flow can result from a malfunctioning bleed‑air valve or a leaking turbine discharge pressure probe/line; verify bleed valve operation and probe/line condition. Finally, high EGT at target takeoff EPR indicates the engine is out of trim; use a jet‑calibrator to re‑trim the engine.
